A Unified Uncertainty Representation for Graph Neural Networks via Doubly-Spectral Stochastic Expansion

Fred Xu ††thanks: Work done during an internship at Block, Inc. Affiliation: Department of Computer Science Affiliation: University of California, Los Angeles Email: fredxu@cs.ucla.edu    Thomas Markovich Affiliation: Block, Inc. Email: tmarkovich@squareup.com    Florence Regol Affiliation: Mila, Quebec AI Institute Email: florence.regol@mila.quebec    Yizhou Sun Affiliation: Department of Computer Science Affiliation: University of California, Los Angeles Email: yzsun@cs.ucla.edu
Abstract

Reliable deployment of graph neural networks requires calibration, out-of-distribution (OOD) detection, and robustness to distribution shift, yet existing methods address these needs with separate models and objectives. We model uncertain node embeddings as random graph signals: graph Fourier filters capture structural variation, and a scalar orthogonal-polynomial chaos coordinate captures latent stochastic variation. The resulting doubly-spectral stochastic (DSS) expansion supplies task-matched readouts from one representation: the mean coefficient encodes class evidence for the energy-based OOD score, the higher-order coefficients encode structured logit variation, and quadrature averaging over the chaos coordinate defines the single predictive distribution used for prediction and calibration. A capacity theorem shows that, under a full-rank feature assumption, a restricted subfamily matches the chaos coefficients of any Gaussian-latent random graph signal, with exponentially decaying truncation error under a growth condition; the task-level claims are established empirically. DSS-GNN has two deployment modes: standalone, or as a residual branch beside a deterministic encoder (DSS-Hybrid). Standalone DSS-GNN achieves the lowest Brier score among the compared uncertainty-aware baselines on all 14 node classification benchmarks without post-hoc correction; DSS-Hybrid achieves the best AUROC on most node-OOD settings, competitive cross-graph OOD detection, and the strongest shifted accuracy on all 7 GOOD concept-shift benchmarks under standard empirical risk minimization (ERM). Cross-evaluating both modes on all three tasks shows that each remains effective on the other’s tasks, with documented exceptions, and yields explicit deployment guidance.

1 Introduction

Graph neural networks (GNNs) perform well on graph-structured data, yet reliable deployment in drug discovery [31], fraud detection [7], or traffic forecasting [18] requires calibrated probabilities, out-of-distribution (OOD) detection, and robustness to distribution shift. On graphs the three needs are coupled, because uncertainty depends on neighborhood structure as well as node features, and they are instances of one question: when, and how confidently, can the model predict? Calibration measures the agreement between confidence and accuracy in distribution (ID), OOD detection requires low confidence outside the training support, and shift robustness requires that accuracy decrease slowly as the input distribution changes. A representation that explicitly encodes predictive uncertainty addresses all three, with calibrated probabilities, OOD evidence, and a regularized residual under shift obtained from one signal. Most existing methods target one requirement: sampling-based uncertainty methods add computational overhead [10, 17, 19]; evidential models such as Graph Posterior Network (GPN) [30] provide OOD evidence but not shift-robust classification, and intrinsic uncertainty models such as G-Δ\DeltaUQ [33] target calibration under shift; energy-based detectors [36, 9] provide separation scores rather than calibrated probabilities; and robust-training methods [27, 1, 38] do not model uncertainty explicitly.

Spectral GNNs learn filters along the graph-frequency axis [6]; we add a second spectral axis for stochastic variation. DSS-GNN represents each node embedding as a polynomial chaos expansion in a scalar Gaussian latent [37] and propagates the joint graph-frequency/chaos-order coefficients through a learnable doubly-spectral layer (Figure 4, Appendix H). One deterministic forward pass gives task-matched readouts: the quadrature-averaged predictive distribution, whose argmax is the point predictor, is used for prediction and calibration, with the higher-order coefficients encoding structured logit variation; the zeroth-order mean logit gives an energy score for OOD detection that retains the common-logit shifts that softmax cancels; and, paired with a deterministic encoder (DSS-Hybrid, e.g., GCN [15]), the DSS branch acts as a regularized low-/high-pass residual under distribution shift. DSS-GNN is thus one uncertainty representation with two deployment modes; Section 4.5 evaluates both on all three tasks and states which to prefer where. Our contributions are:

  1. 1.

    A doubly-spectral stochastic representation for GNNs with a capacity theorem: under a full-rank feature assumption, a restricted DSS subfamily matches the chaos coefficients of any Gaussian-latent random graph signal, with exponentially decaying truncation error for targets with an entire extension of Gaussian growth (Theorem 2). The theorem (Section 3.3) establishes representational capacity, consistent with the empirical plateau at P=1P{=}1–22, but does not by itself guarantee calibration, OOD detection, or robustness, which are supported empirically.

  2. 2.

    A learnable doubly-spectral layer whose quadrature-averaged loss differs from the mean-logit loss by a curvature-weighted correction over the chaos covariance (Proposition 2), relating the chaos coefficients to calibration, bounding the gap between the quadrature predictive and the mean-logit softmax (Corollary 1), and identifying the mean-logit energy as the readout that retains common-logit shifts.

  3. 3.

    Empirically, the lowest Brier score among compared uncertainty-aware baselines on all 14 calibration benchmarks (standalone), the best AUROC on most node-OOD settings with competitive cross-graph OOD, and the strongest shifted accuracy on all 7 concept-shift benchmarks under ERM (hybrid), plus a cross-evaluation of both modes on all three tasks, component-wise ablations (Table 21), and explicit deployment guidance.

2 Background

Spectral GNNs and uncertainty on graphs.

A graph signal on 𝒢=(V,E)\mathcal{G}=(V,E) with NN nodes is a vector x∈ℝNx\in\mathbb{R}^{N} in the Hilbert space ℓ2​(V)\ell^{2}(V); the Laplacian LGL_{G} is self-adjoint and its eigenvectors form the graph Fourier basis [29, 24]. Spectral GNNs define graph convolutions as polynomial filters of LGL_{G}; ChebNet [6] uses g⁡(LG)=∑k=0Kck​Tk​(L~G)g(L_{G})=\sum_{k=0}^{K}c_{k}T_{k}(\widetilde{L}_{G}) with learned coefficients ckc_{k}, Chebyshev polynomials TkT_{k}, and the rescaled Laplacian L~G=2​LG/λmax−I\widetilde{L}_{G}=2L_{G}/\lambda_{\max}-I (λmax\lambda_{\max} the largest eigenvalue), which keeps filtering localized and allows low-pass or high-pass responses under homophily or heterophily [2]. DSS-GNN adds a second spectral axis, chaos order, orthogonal to graph frequency, and embeds uncertainty directly into spectral filtering.

Polynomial chaos and the doubly-spectral expansion.

To organize stochastic variation spectrally, as the graph Fourier basis organizes structural variation, we use polynomial chaos expansion (PCE) [35, 4, 37], classical in uncertainty quantification [23] but, to our knowledge, not previously combined with graph spectral filtering inside a GNN (Appendix A.1 gives a self-contained introduction). PCE represents a square-integrable random variable Y⁡(ω)Y(\omega) as a series in the orthonormal Hermite polynomials {Ψn​(ω)}n≥0\{\Psi_{n}(\omega)\}_{n\geq 0} of a Gaussian latent ω∼𝒩⁡(0,1)\omega\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1); truncating at order PP gives Y⁡(ω)≈∑n=0PYn​Ψn​(ω)Y(\omega)\approx\sum_{n=0}^{P}Y_{n}\Psi_{n}(\omega), where Y0Y_{0} is the mean and ∑n=1PYn2\sum_{n=1}^{P}Y_{n}^{2} (the chaos energy) the variance. Combined with the Laplacian eigenbasis {uj}\{u_{j}\} on ℓ2​(V)\ell^{2}(V), the Hermite basis on L2​(ℝ,γ)L^{2}(\mathbb{R},\gamma) (γ\gamma the standard Gaussian measure) gives a tensor-product representation: a random graph signal determined by ω\omega is in ℓ2​(V)⊗L2​(ℝ,γ)\ell^{2}(V)\otimes L^{2}(\mathbb{R},\gamma) and admits the doubly-spectral stochastic expansion

Y⁡(ω)=∑n=0∞∑j=1Nuj​Y^n,j⊤​Ψn​(ω),Y(\omega)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\sum_{j=1}^{N}u_{j}\,\hat{Y}_{n,j}^{\top}\,\Psi_{n}(\omega), (1)

where Y^n,j∈ℝd\hat{Y}_{n,j}\in\mathbb{R}^{d} is the joint coefficient at graph frequency λj\lambda_{j} (the jj-th Laplacian eigenvalue) and chaos order nn, and dd is the signal dimension; {uj⊗Ψn}\{u_{j}\otimes\Psi_{n}\} is a complete orthonormal basis of this space (Remark 2), ω\omega is scalar, and each chaos coefficient is a dd-dimensional graph signal. DSS-GNN learns a truncation and a propagation rule on this tensor-product space.

3 Method

DSS-GNN instantiates the doubly-spectral expansion (1) as a trainable network by learning a coupled propagation rule for the joint coefficients Y^n,j\hat{Y}_{n,j} through parameterized graph filters and non-intrusive chaos projection (Figure 4, Appendix H).

Intuition.

A random graph signal assigns to each node a random variable with finite second moment. We model all randomness as driven by a single shared standard Gaussian factor ω\omega: every node embedding is a deterministic function of ω\omega, expanded in the Hermite polynomials Ψn​(ω)\Psi_{n}(\omega), which play along the stochastic axis exactly the role that the graph Fourier modes play along the structural axis. A DSS layer therefore stores, for every node, P+1P+1 coefficient vectors (one per chaos order) instead of a single hidden vector; a deterministic embedding is the special case in which only the order-0 coefficient is nonzero. Each layer decomposes the embeddings onto this basis, applies learned filters jointly per graph frequency and per chaos order (dual low/high-pass Chebyshev filters along the graph axis, per-order gates along the chaos axis), and reassembles. The core Gaussian is never materialized: because pointwise nonlinearities mix chaos orders, the layer evaluates the embedding field at SS deterministic Gauss–Hermite nodes, applies the activation there, and projects back onto the Hermite basis. With S≥P+1S\geq P+1 the polynomial filter and gate terms are integrated exactly at the gate orders used in practice (Pg≤1P_{g}\leq 1, Appendix A), and the nonlinearity is handled by a controlled non-intrusive projection (Remark 3), so the network is deterministic end to end: no Monte-Carlo sampling and no sampling variance. The expansion itself requires only the shared Gaussian factor and finite second moments; the exponential truncation rate of Theorem 2 additionally requires targets with an entire (analytic) Gaussian extension. Readouts then select task-appropriate functionals of the same expansion: the quadrature-averaged predictive (8) for prediction and calibration, and the mean-logit energy (9) for OOD scores.

3.1 DSS layer

Let 𝒢=(V,E)\mathcal{G}=(V,E) have N=|V|N=|V| nodes, features X∈ℝN×dinX\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times d_{\rm in}}, and Laplacian LGL_{G}. DSS-GNN stacks LL layers on a truncated expansion at chaos order PP; the input is lifted by Hn(0)=X​Win(n)H_{n}^{(0)}=XW_{\mathrm{in}}^{(n)} with Win(n)∈ℝdin×d0W_{\mathrm{in}}^{(n)}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\rm in}\times d_{0}}, and at layer ℓ∈{0,…,L−1}\ell\in\{0,\dots,L{-}1\} the embeddings are

H(ℓ)​(ω)=∑n=0PHn(ℓ)​Ψn​(ω),Hn(ℓ)∈ℝN×dℓ,H^{(\ell)}(\omega)=\sum_{n=0}^{P}H_{n}^{(\ell)}\Psi_{n}(\omega),\qquad H_{n}^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times d_{\ell}}, (2)

with dℓd_{\ell} the hidden width, so each node maintains P+1P{+}1 coefficient-valued hidden states. The layer updates them along both spectral axes. Along the graph-frequency axis, dual Chebyshev filters propagate each coefficient through localized low-pass and high-pass branches,

Glp​(LG)=∑k=0Klpck(lp)​Tk​(L~G),Ghp​(LG)=∑k=0Khpck(hp)​Tk​(L~G),G_{\mathrm{lp}}(L_{G})=\sum_{k=0}^{K_{\mathrm{lp}}}c_{k}^{(\mathrm{lp})}T_{k}(\widetilde{L}_{G}),\qquad G_{\mathrm{hp}}(L_{G})=\sum_{k=0}^{K_{\mathrm{hp}}}c_{k}^{(\mathrm{hp})}T_{k}(\widetilde{L}_{G}), (3)

with filter degrees Klp,KhpK_{\mathrm{lp}},K_{\mathrm{hp}} and learned coefficients ck(lp),ck(hp)∈ℝc_{k}^{(\mathrm{lp})},c_{k}^{(\mathrm{hp})}\in\mathbb{R}. Along the chaos-order axis, per-order chaos gates αn​(ω),βn​(ω)\alpha_{n}(\omega),\beta_{n}(\omega) couple the two branches; they are deterministic scalars or low-order chaos expansions of gate order PgP_{g} with learnable an,r,bn,r∈ℝa_{n,r},b_{n,r}\in\mathbb{R}:

αn​(ω)=∑r=0Pgan,r​Ψr​(ω),βn​(ω)=∑r=0Pgbn,r​Ψr​(ω).\alpha_{n}(\omega)=\textstyle\sum_{r=0}^{P_{g}}a_{n,r}\Psi_{r}(\omega),\qquad\beta_{n}(\omega)=\textstyle\sum_{r=0}^{P_{g}}b_{n,r}\Psi_{r}(\omega). (4)

Because pointwise nonlinearities mix chaos orders, the update has no closed form. A non-intrusive projection evaluates the field at SS Gauss–Hermite nodes {(ωs,μs)}s=1S\{(\omega_{s},\mu_{s})\}_{s=1}^{S} (nodes ωs∈ℝ\omega_{s}\in\mathbb{R}, weights μs>0\mu_{s}>0), applies the activation σ\sigma, and projects back:

H~(ℓ+1)​(ωs)\displaystyle\widetilde{H}^{(\ell+1)}(\omega_{s}) =(∑n=0PΨn​(ωs)​(αn​(ωs)​Glp​(LG)​Hn(ℓ)+βn​(ωs)​Ghp​(LG)​Hn(ℓ)))​Wℓ.\displaystyle=\Bigg(\sum_{n=0}^{P}\Psi_{n}(\omega_{s})\Big(\alpha_{n}(\omega_{s})G_{\mathrm{lp}}(L_{G})H_{n}^{(\ell)}+\beta_{n}(\omega_{s})G_{\mathrm{hp}}(L_{G})H_{n}^{(\ell)}\Big)\Bigg)W_{\ell}. (5)
Hm(ℓ+1)=∑s=1Sμsσ(H~(ℓ+1)(ωs))Ψm(ωs),m=0,…,P,H_{m}^{(\ell+1)}=\sum_{s=1}^{S}\mu_{s}\,\sigma\!\big(\widetilde{H}^{(\ell+1)}(\omega_{s})\big)\Psi_{m}(\omega_{s}),\qquad m=0,\dots,P, (6)

with Wℓ∈ℝdℓ×dℓ+1W_{\ell}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\ell}\times d_{\ell+1}} trainable (quadrature details in Appendix A.1; notation in Table 30, Appendix H).

3.2 Uncertainty readout

After LL layers a linear readout Wout∈ℝdL×CW_{\mathrm{out}}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{L}\times C} (CC classes, labels yi∈{1,…,C}y_{i}\in\{1,\dots,C\}) produces per-order logit coefficients Zi,n:=(Hn(L)​Wout)i∈ℝCZ_{i,n}:=(H_{n}^{(L)}W_{\mathrm{out}})_{i}\in\mathbb{R}^{C} for node ii. The mean logit Zi,0Z_{i,0} encodes the zeroth-order class evidence used by the energy score; the logit covariance and chaos energy are

Σzi=∑n=1PZi,n​Zi,n⊤∈ℝC×C,ℰi=tr⁡(Σzi)=∑n=1P‖Zi,n‖2.\Sigma_{z_{i}}=\sum_{n=1}^{P}Z_{i,n}Z_{i,n}^{\top}\in\mathbb{R}^{C\times C},\qquad\mathcal{E}_{i}=\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma_{z_{i}})=\sum_{n=1}^{P}\|Z_{i,n}\|^{2}. (7)

The quadrature logits zi(s)=∑n=0PZi,n​Ψn​(ωs)z_{i}^{(s)}=\sum_{n=0}^{P}Z_{i,n}\Psi_{n}(\omega_{s}) are deterministic evaluations of the learned expansion (no Gaussian noise is injected in training or inference) and define the readouts. The quadrature-averaged predictive

p¯i=∑s=1Sμs​softmax​(zi(s))∈ℝC\bar{p}_{i}=\sum_{s=1}^{S}\mu_{s}\,\mathrm{softmax}(z_{i}^{(s)})\in\mathbb{R}^{C} (8)

is the model’s predictive distribution and the point prediction is its argmax, y^i=arg⁡maxc⁡p¯i,c\hat{y}_{i}=\arg\max_{c}\bar{p}_{i,c}, so prediction and calibration are two functionals of one distribution. Its deviation from the mean-logit softmax is bounded by the chaos covariance, ‖p¯i−softmax⁡(Zi,0)‖∞≤B2​tr⁡(Σzi)\|\bar{p}_{i}-\mathrm{softmax}(Z_{i,0})\|_{\infty}\leq\tfrac{B}{2}\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma_{z_{i}}) for a universal constant BB (Corollary 1), which training keeps small (Section 3.5); Section 4.2 measures the agreement. For OOD detection, the energy score [20]

senergy(i)=−log∑c=1Cexp(Zi,0,c),s_{\mathrm{energy}}(i)=-\log\sum_{c=1}^{C}\exp(Z_{i,0,c}), (9)

with Zi,0,cZ_{i,0,c} the cc-th mean logit, captures confidence in the mean prediction; predictive entropy and mutual information of the quadrature softmaxes are auxiliary summaries of the same readout. The OOD experiments use the energy score with graph propagation, following GNNSafe [36].

3.3 Theoretical properties

Four results connect the layer to the expansion (1); proofs are in Appendix A.

Proposition 1 (Generalization).

With P=0P=0 and Pg=0P_{g}=0, (2) has a single deterministic coefficient H0(ℓ)H_{0}^{(\ell)} with scalar gates, and the DSS layer reduces to a standard polynomial spectral GNN layer, recovering ChebNet, GCN, and related models as special cases.

Theorem 1 (Doubly-spectral operator).

With the pointwise nonlinearity omitted, gates of chaos degree at most PgP_{g}, states of degree at most PP, and a Gauss–Hermite rule exact for all triple products Ψr​Ψn​Ψm\Psi_{r}\Psi_{n}\Psi_{m} (r≤Pgr\leq P_{g}; n,m≤Pn,m\leq P; S≥⌈(Pg+2​P+1)/2⌉S\geq\lceil(P_{g}+2P+1)/2\rceil suffices), the linearized DSS layer is a linear operator on the joint graph-frequency/chaos-order domain of (1), acting frequency by frequency: the Chebyshev filters set the graph-frequency response and the chaos gates the chaos-order mixing (Appendix A.4; the omitted nonlinearity’s projection error is decomposed in Proposition 3).

Theorem 2 (Representational capacity and truncation under full-rank features).

Let 𝒢\mathcal{G} have NN nodes and features X∈ℝN×dinX\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times d_{\rm in}} with rank⁡(X)=N\operatorname{rank}(X)=N (which requires din≥Nd_{\rm in}\geq N). With ReLU activation, a restricted subfamily of DSS-GNNs (one layer, lifted width 2​d​(P+1)2d(P{+}1), quadrature size S=P+1S=P{+}1, constant gates, identity low-pass filter) has the following properties. For any target Y∈L2​(ℝ,γ,ℝN×d)Y\in L^{2}(\mathbb{R},\gamma;\mathbb{R}^{N\times d}) and any chaos order PP, some output Y~P\widetilde{Y}_{P} matches the chaos coefficients of YY through order PP; letting PP and width vary, the resulting outputs are dense in L2​(ℝ,γ,ℝN×d)L^{2}(\mathbb{R},\gamma;\mathbb{R}^{N\times d}). If YY in addition admits an entire Gaussian extension with controlled growth (Appendix A.6), the truncation error decays exponentially:

‖Y−Y~P‖L2​(ℝ,γ,ℝN×d)≤Ctr​βP\|Y-\widetilde{Y}_{P}\|_{L^{2}(\mathbb{R},\gamma;\,\mathbb{R}^{N\times d})}\leq C_{\rm tr}\,\beta^{P} (10)

for some Ctr>0C_{\rm tr}>0 and β∈(0,1)\beta\in(0,1) depending on YY.

Theorems 1 and 2 are capacity statements: they establish the operator structure and the representational capacity of the layer and identify no inherent expressivity obstruction, but they do not by themselves guarantee calibration, OOD detection, or robustness, which are empirical claims supported task by task in Section 4. The full-rank case requires din≥Nd_{\rm in}\geq N; for rank⁡(X)<N\operatorname{rank}(X)<N, the common case (Cora has 1,433 features for 2,708 nodes), Remark 5 shows that the same construction still matches every truncated target whose chaos-coefficient columns lie in range⁡(X)\operatorname{range}(X), under one positivity condition satisfiable by appending a constant feature column.

Proposition 2 (Stochastic and mean-logit readouts).

Assume the number of Gauss–Hermite quadrature nodes is at least one more than the chaos order, and that the per-node loss ℓ⁡(⋅,yi)\ell(\cdot,y_{i}) satisfies the regularity conditions in Lemma 3. Then:

  1. 1.

    (Calibration channel.) The per-node quadrature-averaged loss ℓ¯i:=∑s=1Sμs​ℓ​(zi(s),yi)\bar{\ell}_{i}:=\sum_{s=1}^{S}\mu_{s}\,\ell(z_{i}^{(s)},y_{i}) admits the Taylor expansion ℓ¯i=ℓ⁡(Zi,0,yi)+12​tr⁡(ℋi​Σzi)+O⁡(maxs⁡‖zi(s)−Zi,0‖3),\bar{\ell}_{i}=\ell(Z_{i,0},y_{i})+\tfrac{1}{2}\operatorname{tr}(\mathcal{H}_{i}\,\Sigma_{z_{i}})+O\!\big(\max_{s}\|z_{i}^{(s)}-Z_{i,0}\|^{3}\big), where ℋi=∇z2​ℓ​(Zi,0,yi)\mathcal{H}_{i}=\nabla_{z}^{2}\ell(Z_{i,0},y_{i}) is the loss Hessian and Σzi\Sigma_{z_{i}} is the chaos covariance (7).

  2. 2.

    (OOD channel.) Shifting every class logit by the same constant leaves the softmax output, and hence any softmax-derived summary such as predictive entropy or mutual information, unchanged; by contrast, the energy score (9) decreases by exactly that constant.

Calibration: the curvature-weighted term 12​tr⁡(ℋi​Σzi)\tfrac{1}{2}\operatorname{tr}(\mathcal{H}_{i}\Sigma_{z_{i}}) is the leading-order difference between the quadrature-averaged and the mean-logit objectives; it weights the chaos covariance by the loss curvature and, for cross-entropy, is at most 14​ℰi\tfrac{1}{4}\mathcal{E}_{i}, the quantity that (11) regularizes; no post-hoc temperature scaling is used. The same expansion applied to the softmax readout bounds the gap between p¯i\bar{p}_{i} and softmax⁡(Zi,0)\mathrm{softmax}(Z_{i,0}) by the chaos covariance (Corollary 1), which the objective keeps small; the calibration gains of P>0P>0 therefore arise through training rather than a readout-time correction, and the two trained readouts agree closely (Section 4.2). OOD detection: the energy score is linear in a common logit shift, while softmax-derived summaries cancel it, so an OOD input that uniformly lowers the class-evidence logits changes the energy but not the entropy; Section 4.3 confirms that detection is insensitive to the chaos order, as this readout predicts.

3.4 Hybrid deployment

Distribution shift weakens the common-evidence signal and changes which graph frequencies are predictive; like OOD detection it requires a strong deterministic predictor on seen structure paired with a regularized residual that accounts for cross-distribution variability. DSS-Hybrid adds DSS-GNN as a residual branch beside a deterministic base encoder with one shared class readout, zi,0hyb=zibase+γres​Zi,0z_{i,0}^{\mathrm{hyb}}=z_{i}^{\mathrm{base}}+\gamma_{\mathrm{res}}Z_{i,0}, with zibase∈ℝCz_{i}^{\mathrm{base}}\in\mathbb{R}^{C} the base logit and γres∈ℝ\gamma_{\mathrm{res}}\in\mathbb{R} a learned scale (lowercase for post-combination logits, uppercase Zi,nZ_{i,n} for the DSS coefficients); the quadrature logits combine the same way, zihyb,(s)=zibase+γres​∑n=0PZi,n​Ψn​(ωs)z_{i}^{\mathrm{hyb},(s)}=z_{i}^{\mathrm{base}}+\gamma_{\mathrm{res}}\sum_{n=0}^{P}Z_{i,n}\Psi_{n}(\omega_{s}), so the readouts of Section 3.2 transfer directly. The chaos-energy regularizer keeps the residual from fitting in-distribution noise, so its dual filters retain capacity for shifts in graph-frequency response and its mean logit remains a common-evidence channel for the energy score. The base encoder, a 2-layer GCN for fair comparison with baselines, is warmed up before the DSS branch is activated. This design is an inductive bias rather than a distribution-free guarantee.

3.5 Training and downstream tasks

Both modes are trained with the chaos-energy-regularized mean-logit loss

ℒbase=1|𝒱tr|​∑i∈𝒱trℓ⁡(Zi,0,yi)+λreg​1|𝒱tr|​∑i∈𝒱trℰi,\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{base}}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{tr}}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{tr}}}\ell(Z_{i,0},\,y_{i})\;+\;\lambda_{\mathrm{reg}}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{tr}}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{tr}}}\mathcal{E}_{i}, (11)

with 𝒱tr\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{tr}} the training nodes, ℓ\ell the per-node cross-entropy, and λreg≥0\lambda_{\mathrm{reg}}\geq 0; for DSS-Hybrid, Zi,0Z_{i,0} is replaced by zi,0hybz_{i,0}^{\mathrm{hyb}} and the regularizer applies to the DSS coefficients only. Only the mean logit is supervised, but the projection update (6) couples Zi,0Z_{i,0} to all chaos orders, so the higher-order coefficients are trained implicitly while the regularizer constrains their variation. By Proposition 2, ℒbase\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{base}} agrees to first order with the quadrature-averaged loss ℒquad\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{quad}} (35) of Appendix D; we use ℒbase\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{base}} throughout. The trace that Corollary 1 bounds is the regularized chaos energy ℰi\mathcal{E}_{i}; where the selected λreg\lambda_{\mathrm{reg}} is small or zero, the measured readout gap remains small (Table 27).

4 Experiments

4.1 Setup

For calibration, standalone DSS-GNN is compared with TFE-GNN [8] and G-Δ\DeltaUQ [33] on 14 node classification benchmarks [15, 28, 25, 26], reporting accuracy and the Brier score [3] over 10 splits without post-hoc calibration. For OOD detection, DSS-Hybrid is evaluated on the GNNSafe benchmark [36] (nine node-OOD settings on Cora, Amazon-Photo, and Coauthor-CS, plus cross-graph Twitch and Arxiv; 3 seeds) against GNNSafe, GNNSafe++, and GPN [30] at the values reported by Wu et al. [36], and against Graph-EBM [9] (scored with its own diffusion), MC-dropout (M=20M{=}20) [10] and Deep Ensembles (M=5M{=}5) [17] on the same GCN backbone with the same score propagation. For distribution shift, DSS-Hybrid is trained with empirical risk minimization (ERM) on 7 concept-shift settings of GOOD [12] and compared with the 12 GOOD/TAR baselines [1, 27, 38] and G-Δ\DeltaUQ. Point predictions are arg⁡max⁡p¯i\arg\max\bar{p}_{i} (Section 3.2); Table 1 reports the mean-logit readout, which Section 4.2 shows to agree with it. All experiments use ℒbase\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{base}} (11); in the OOD experiments DSS-Hybrid, like GNNSafe++, adds the GNNSafe++ energy-margin regularizer at per-dataset margins. Baselines, datasets, and configurations are in Appendices B–D; code is available at https://github.com/heraclixus/DSSGNN.

4.2 Node classification and calibration

Table 1 shows that DSS-GNN achieves the lowest Brier score among the compared uncertainty-aware baselines on all 14 datasets, homophilous and heterophilous, without post-hoc calibration, and the best accuracy on 13. The Brier gains over the deterministic P=0P=0 arm are largest on Citeseer, Texas, and Minesweeper (Table 14), consistent with the curvature-weighted correction of Proposition 2. This is not an accuracy effect: standard GNNs match or exceed DSS-GNN in accuracy on Cora and Citeseer while remaining less calibrated (Appendix F), and at P=0P=0 DSS-GNN is a competitive dual-filter spectral GNN (Proposition 1), so the gains are attributable to the chaos expansion (Table 19). Figure 1 visualizes the correction ci=12​tr⁡(ℋi​Σzi)c_{i}=\tfrac{1}{2}\operatorname{tr}(\mathcal{H}_{i}\Sigma_{z_{i}}) on Minesweeper: it is largest where stochastic variation aligns with high-curvature directions and concentrates on the hardest nodes.

Prediction and calibration use one predictive distribution.

Under the full protocol with both readouts evaluated at the same checkpoints, arg⁡max⁡p¯i\arg\max\bar{p}_{i} and arg⁡max⁡Zi,0\arg\max Z_{i,0} disagree on at most 0.21%0.21\% of test nodes (exactly zero on 10 of 14 datasets), with accuracy within 0.040.04 points and Brier within 0.0030.003 (Table 27, Appendix G); in hybrid mode the disagreement is 0.00000.0000 on all 14 datasets. The agreement is structural: for S≥P+1S\geq P{+}1 Corollary 1 bounds the readout gap by tr⁡(Σzi)\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma_{z_{i}}), which the objective keeps small (Section 3.5), so the reported calibration is that of the distribution the predictions are drawn from.

Chaos order.

Sweeping P∈{0,…,6,8}P\in\{0,\dots,6,8\} (Appendix E, Figure 3) improves Brier on 12 of 14 datasets at P>0P>0, and at least one of P=1P=1 or P=2P=2 is within 0.020.02 Brier of the best swept order on every dataset, consistent with the exponential truncation bound of Theorem 2. PP is selected per dataset on validation Brier (Table 12); the larger selected orders are near-ties rather than requirements, and we recommend P=1​–​2P=1\text{--}2 as the default. Within the shared-factor family P=1P=1 is exactly a Gaussian embedding; the higher orders add non-Gaussian structure (Citeseer Brier 0.3460.346 to 0.3080.308 at P=2P=2; Tables 13–14).

4.3 OOD detection

Tables 2–3 compare DSS-Hybrid with GNNSafe++ [36], the strongest OOD baseline: it has the best AUROC on 6 of 9 node-OOD cells (Cora 94.32/97.60/94.1194.32/97.60/94.11 versus 90.62/95.56/92.7590.62/95.56/92.75 for structure/feature/label; Amazon-Photo feature/label 99.66/97.5299.66/97.52; Coauthor-CS label 98.0798.07) and is within 0.130.13 points of the best method on the three remaining cells, where both it and GNNSafe++ exceed 99.699.6. On Twitch it improves over GNNSafe++ on every metric (AUROC 95.7595.75 vs 95.3695.36, FPR95 22.4022.40 vs 33.5733.57); on Arxiv it gives the best FPR95 and ID accuracy while remaining within 1.411.41 AUROC points of GNNSafe++ (73.3673.36 vs 74.7774.77). DSS-Hybrid follows the GNNSafe++ protocol (same GCN backbone configuration, energy-margin objective with its per-dataset margins, and score propagation; Appendix D), so the two differ in the DSS residual branch. Against MC-dropout and Deep Ensembles, which receive the same propagation, DSS-Hybrid has the higher AUROC on all 11 settings in one forward pass versus their 20 passes and 5 models; the published GPN values are below GNNSafe++ throughout.

Detection comes from the energy readout, with propagation, acting on the DSS mean logit (9), which Proposition 2 formalizes as the readout that retains common-evidence shifts. Under this identical readout the DSS representation separates ID from OOD more widely than the GCN encoder alone (the Cora columns of Table 2), and a controlled ablation that varies only the chaos order P∈{0,…,3}P\in\{0,\dots,3\} at one fixed configuration leaves energy AUROC flat (Cora-structure 91.0/91.2/90.9/90.891.0/91.2/90.9/90.8; the level differs from Table 2 as the ablation is a separate set of runs; Appendix E), as the design predicts since the energy score reads the mean logit alone. Score propagation contributes up to +18.2+18.2 AUROC (Twitch) and +14.5+14.5 (Cora-structure) at identical checkpoints (Appendix E). Figure 2 shows the resulting wider energy-density gap between ID and OOD modes relative to the energy-based baselines.

4.4 Distribution-shifted classification

The GOOD benchmark [12] tests generalization under distribution shift. Table 4 compares DSS-Hybrid, trained with standard ERM, against the GOOD/TAR baselines and G-Δ\DeltaUQ on seven concept-shift settings (covariate-shift splits in Appendix G.7): it has the best mean shifted accuracy in every case, by margins from 0.080.08 (GOOD-Cora/word) to 9.949.94 points (GOOD-WebKB/university). This is consistent with the inductive bias of Section 3.4: the regularized low-/high-pass residual can model the shift in which graph frequencies are predictive while the base predictor is preserved. Section 4.5 isolates the residual pathway as a unit (hybrid versus its identically trained GCN base), and Appendix E (Table 15) isolates the chaos order under shift: at the validation-selected standalone configurations, P=1P{=}1 improves shifted accuracy over P=0P{=}0 on GOOD-Cora/word (+1.7+1.7), GOOD-Cora/degree (+1.2+1.2), and GOOD-Arxiv/time (+0.6+0.6), so on those settings the uncertainty representation, not only the dual-filter structure, contributes.

4.5 Standalone versus hybrid: cross-evaluation and deployment guidance

Each mode is also evaluated on the other’s tasks under the same protocols. Table 5 summarizes the outcome, and Tables 24–26 in Appendix G give the per-dataset numbers with standard deviations and ID accuracies (protocols in Appendix G.1).

Classification and calibration.

The standalone is the stronger calibrated classifier on 13 of 14 datasets; Tolokers is the one exception (hybrid 81.281.2 accuracy / 0.2550.255 Brier versus 79.979.9 / 0.2680.268). Where the GCN encoder is strong the two are close (Cora 86.686.6 vs 84.384.3); on heterophilous graphs the DSS residual compensates for a weak encoder (Roman-Empire 78.878.8 vs 74.474.4); and where a plain GCN is unsuitable the standalone is higher (Texas 91.391.3 vs 45.645.6, Squirrel 68.168.1 vs 26.426.4). Against its own identically trained GCN base, the hybrid never loses beyond noise on either metric (worst accuracy delta −0.8-0.8 on Texas, inside one standard deviation of 7.77.7) and gains where the encoder is weak (Roman-Empire +27.7+27.7 accuracy / −0.33-0.33 Brier, Minesweeper +6.6+6.6 / −0.11-0.11): the residual never measurably reduces its encoder’s calibration or clean accuracy, and where the base is unsuitable (small heterophilous graphs) the hybrid matches it rather than improving on it.

OOD detection.

The hybrid is the stronger detector on 10 of 11 settings. Its GCN-plus-residual encoder is stronger in the sparse-label perturbation regime (Cora-structure 94.394.3 vs 79.879.8) and for cross-graph transfer (Twitch), while on Arxiv the standalone run under the GNNSafe++ margin objective is 0.40.4 higher with the best Arxiv ID accuracy (61.261.2 vs 54.054.0). The one standalone exception is Twitch: the classifier trains (ID accuracy 68.468.4 vs 70.570.5) but its energy score does not separate the cross-graph OOD inputs, so the hybrid (95.895.8) is preferred there. On the perturbation settings with tiny public splits the GNNSafe pipeline gives every backbone BatchNorm, and plain GCN in the same pipeline does not train without it (ID accuracy 75.775.7 with BatchNorm, 45.845.8 without, on Cora-structure); the standalone uses one BatchNorm1d per chaos channel (Appendix D) in all OOD and GOOD cells but OOD Twitch and GOOD-Arxiv/degree, and does not need it under the full-label calibration protocol (Appendix G.6).

Distribution shift.

On GOOD the standalone is above every baseline of Table 4 on 5 of 7 settings (WebKB 36.436.4 and Twitch 60.360.3 vs TAR 30.830.8 and 57.257.2) and at ERM’s level on the other two (CBAS 82.482.4, Arxiv/time 65.465.4), with ID accuracy between 63.563.5 and 96.296.2 (Appendix G); the hybrid is above every baseline on all 7.

Deployment guidance.

The two modes share one uncertainty representation and the same two readouts, (8) and (9), and differ in the encoder. Outside the exceptions above, each is the better mode on its deployment task and remains effective on the other’s. We recommend the standalone for calibration-critical single-graph use, in particular under heterophily, and the hybrid when a strong conventional encoder exists, for cross-graph transfer, and for OOD detection in sparse-label regimes; the standalone requires BatchNorm stabilization in sparse-label regimes, and the hybrid shares its encoder’s failures (Section 5).

5 Conclusion and Limitations

DSS-GNN is one uncertainty representation, a doubly-spectral stochastic expansion over graph-frequency and chaos-order axes, with task-matched readouts and two deployment modes. Empirically, the standalone has the lowest Brier score among the compared uncertainty-aware baselines on all 14 calibration benchmarks, the hybrid the strongest AUROC on most node-OOD settings and the strongest shifted accuracy on all 7 concept-shift benchmarks under ERM, and both modes are effective on all three tasks with the exceptions noted in Section 4.5.

Limitations.

(i) Two deployment modes. The modes share one representation and the same readouts but are not interchangeable in every regime. The standalone model requires BatchNorm stabilization in sparse-label regimes, where every baseline backbone in the OOD pipeline also uses it, and uses it on 6 of 7 GOOD settings; under the full-label calibration protocol it is not needed and is not used (Appendix G.6). The hybrid is preferable when a strong conventional encoder exists and shares that encoder’s limits: on small heterophilous graphs the hybrid matches its base without improving on it. The standalone energy score does not separate cross-graph OOD inputs on Twitch, where only the hybrid is effective. (ii) Scalar latent. All stochastic variation is due to one shared Gaussian factor, perfectly dependent across nodes, so the logit covariance across nodes has rank at most PP. This suffices for the marginal readouts used here (per-node calibration and energy scores) and is what makes single-pass quadrature possible, but it cannot represent independent per-node noise, so joint cross-node uncertainty is not modeled; the sampling baselines (MC-dropout, Deep Ensembles) have higher Brier than the standalone and lower AUROC than the hybrid (Appendix F, Table 2). A vector latent of dimension qq would cost SqS^{q} quadrature nodes on a full tensor grid, which sparse grids mitigate; we leave this to future work. (iii) Compute. The chaos expansion adds a (P+1)×S(P{+}1)\times S operation count per layer; the measured per-epoch overhead at P=2P{=}2 is 2.9×2.9\times on Cora and 1.2×1.2\times on Amazon-Ratings, and about 4%4\% per additional order on ogbn-arxiv, with memory linear in P+1P{+}1 (Table 20).

Appendix A Proofs and Derivations

We begin with a self-contained introduction to Wiener chaos and Gauss–Hermite quadrature (Appendix A.1), then present supporting technical results (Appendix A.2), followed by individual proofs of each main-text theorem (Appendices A.3–A.7).

A.1 Background: Wiener chaos and Gauss–Hermite quadrature

This section collects the probability and approximation theory underlying the doubly-spectral expansion. The material is classical; we follow the presentation in Janson [14] and Xiu and Karniadakis [37]. This appendix is self-contained.

Gaussian measure and Hermite polynomials.

Let γ\gamma denote the standard Gaussian measure on ℝ\mathbb{R}, i.e., dγ(ω)=(2π)−1/2e−ω2/2dωd\gamma(\omega)=(2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-\omega^{2}/2}\,d\omega. The Hilbert space L2​(ℝ,γ)L^{2}(\mathbb{R},\gamma) consists of all square-integrable functions with respect to γ\gamma, equipped with the inner product ⟨f,g⟩=∫ℝf⁡(ω)​g​(ω)​𝑑γ​(ω)=𝔼⁡[f⁡(ω)​g​(ω)]\langle f,g\rangle=\int_{\mathbb{R}}f(\omega)\,g(\omega)\,d\gamma(\omega)=\mathbb{E}[f(\omega)\,g(\omega)] where ω∼𝒩⁡(0,1)\omega\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1).

The probabilists’ Hermite polynomials [32] are defined by the Rodrigues formula

Hen(ω)=(−1)neω2/2dnd​ωne−ω2/2,n=0,1,2,…\mathrm{He}_{n}(\omega)=(-1)^{n}\,e^{\omega^{2}/2}\,\frac{d^{n}}{d\omega^{n}}\,e^{-\omega^{2}/2},\qquad n=0,1,2,\ldots (12)

The first few are He0​(ω)=1\mathrm{He}_{0}(\omega)=1, He1​(ω)=ω\mathrm{He}_{1}(\omega)=\omega, He2​(ω)=ω2−1\mathrm{He}_{2}(\omega)=\omega^{2}-1, He3​(ω)=ω3−3​ω\mathrm{He}_{3}(\omega)=\omega^{3}-3\omega. They satisfy the three-term recurrence

Hen+1​(ω)=ω​Hen​(ω)−n​Hen−1​(ω),\mathrm{He}_{n+1}(\omega)=\omega\,\mathrm{He}_{n}(\omega)-n\,\mathrm{He}_{n-1}(\omega), (13)

with He−1=0\mathrm{He}_{-1}=0, and the orthogonality relation 𝔼⁡[Hem​(ω)​Hen​(ω)]=n!​δm​n\mathbb{E}[\mathrm{He}_{m}(\omega)\,\mathrm{He}_{n}(\omega)]=n!\,\delta_{mn}. Normalizing gives the orthonormal Hermite basis

Ψn​(ω):=Hen​(ω)n!,𝔼⁡[Ψm​Ψn]=δm​n,\Psi_{n}(\omega):=\frac{\mathrm{He}_{n}(\omega)}{\sqrt{n!}},\qquad\mathbb{E}[\Psi_{m}\Psi_{n}]=\delta_{mn}, (14)

which forms a complete orthonormal system for L2​(ℝ,γ)L^{2}(\mathbb{R},\gamma) [32, 14]. Every f∈L2​(ℝ,γ)f\in L^{2}(\mathbb{R},\gamma) can therefore be expanded as f⁡(ω)=∑n=0∞fn​Ψn​(ω)f(\omega)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}f_{n}\,\Psi_{n}(\omega) with fn=𝔼⁡[f​Ψn]f_{n}=\mathbb{E}[f\Psi_{n}] and Parseval’s identity ‖f‖L2​(γ)2=∑nfn2\|f\|_{L^{2}(\gamma)}^{2}=\sum_{n}f_{n}^{2}.

Wiener–Itô chaos decomposition.

The Hermite expansion generalizes to a fundamental structural result in Gaussian analysis. Let (Ω,ℱ,ℙ)(\Omega,\mathcal{F},\mathbb{P}) be a probability space carrying a standard Gaussian random variable ω\omega, and define the associated Gaussian subspace

Lω2:={f⁡(ω):f∈L2​(ℝ,γ)}⊆L2​(Ω,ℙ).L_{\omega}^{2}:=\{f(\omega):f\in L^{2}(\mathbb{R},\gamma)\}\subseteq L^{2}(\Omega,\mathbb{P}).

Define the nn-th Wiener chaos 𝒞n\mathcal{C}_{n} as the closed linear span of Ψn​(ω)\Psi_{n}(\omega) in Lω2L_{\omega}^{2}. Since we use a single Gaussian latent (q=1q=1), each 𝒞n\mathcal{C}_{n} is one-dimensional and spanned by Ψn​(ω)\Psi_{n}(\omega); with q>1q>1, the corresponding chaos subspace would be indexed by Hermite multi-indices. The Wiener–Itô chaos decomposition states [35, 4, 14]:

Lω2=⨁n=0∞𝒞n,L_{\omega}^{2}=\bigoplus_{n=0}^{\infty}\mathcal{C}_{n}, (15)

that is, every square-integrable random variable measurable with respect to ω\omega admits a unique, orthogonal expansion in the Hermite basis. Denoting the orthogonal projection onto 𝒞n\mathcal{C}_{n} by PnP_{n}, any f∈Lω2f\in L_{\omega}^{2} satisfies f=∑n=0∞Pn​ff=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}P_{n}f with ‖f‖2=∑n‖Pn​f‖2\|f\|^{2}=\sum_{n}\|P_{n}f\|^{2}. The zeroth chaos 𝒞0\mathcal{C}_{0} consists of constants (P0​f=𝔼⁡[f]P_{0}f=\mathbb{E}[f]); the first chaos is the space of centered Gaussian random variables; higher chaoses capture progressively more complex nonlinear functionals of ω\omega.

Remark 1 (Analogy with graph spectral decomposition).

The decomposition (15) is the stochastic counterpart of the graph spectral decomposition ℓ2​(V)=⨁j=1Nspan⁡(uj)\ell^{2}(V)=\bigoplus_{j=1}^{N}\mathrm{span}(u_{j}). Both decompose a Hilbert space into eigenspaces of a self-adjoint operator: the graph Laplacian LGL_{G} for ℓ2​(V)\ell^{2}(V), and the Ornstein–Uhlenbeck operator ℒ\mathcal{L} (defined below) for the Gaussian Hilbert space Lω2L_{\omega}^{2}.

Remark 2 (Completeness of the doubly-spectral basis).

Take the signal domain to be the random graph signals generated by the shared latent: a random variable per node with finite second moment, measurable with respect to ω\omega, i.e. an element of the tensor-product Hilbert space ℓ2​(V)⊗L2​(ℝ,γ)\ell^{2}(V)\otimes L^{2}(\mathbb{R},\gamma). The graph Fourier eigenvectors {uj}j=1N\{u_{j}\}_{j=1}^{N} form an orthonormal basis of ℓ2​(V)\ell^{2}(V) and, by the Wiener–Itô decomposition (15), the normalized Hermite polynomials {Ψn}n≥0\{\Psi_{n}\}_{n\geq 0} form an orthonormal basis of L2​(ℝ,γ)L^{2}(\mathbb{R},\gamma). The tensor product of orthonormal bases is an orthonormal basis of the tensor-product space, so {uj⊗Ψn}j≤N,n≥0\{u_{j}\otimes\Psi_{n}\}_{j\leq N,\,n\geq 0} is a complete orthonormal basis of this domain, and the double expansion (1) is a bi-spectral decomposition in the strict sense: both factors are eigenbases of self-adjoint operators (Remark 1). The scope caveat is that the space is built over the scalar ω\omega: signals with independent per-node latents are outside it (Section 5).

The Ornstein–Uhlenbeck operator and hypercontractivity.

The Ornstein–Uhlenbeck (O-U) operator ℒ\mathcal{L} is defined on its standard dense domain in L2​(ℝ,γ)L^{2}(\mathbb{R},\gamma) by

ℒ​f​(ω)=f′′​(ω)−ω​f′​(ω),\mathcal{L}f(\omega)=f^{\prime\prime}(\omega)-\omega\,f^{\prime}(\omega), (16)

with eigenvalues and eigenfunctions ℒ​Ψn=−n​Ψn\mathcal{L}\Psi_{n}=-n\,\Psi_{n} [22]. This is directly analogous to the graph Laplacian having eigenpairs (uj,λj)(u_{j},\lambda_{j}): −ℒ-\mathcal{L} is the corresponding operator on L2​(ℝ,γ)L^{2}(\mathbb{R},\gamma), with the chaos orders 0,1,2,…0,1,2,\ldots as eigenvalues. The associated O-U semigroup Tt=et​ℒT_{t}=e^{t\mathcal{L}} acts as Tt​Ψn=e−n​t​ΨnT_{t}\Psi_{n}=e^{-nt}\Psi_{n}, damping higher-order chaos components exponentially.

A fundamental property of TtT_{t} is hypercontractivity: for 1<p≤q1<p\leq q and e2​t≥(q−1)/(p−1)e^{2t}\geq(q-1)/(p-1),

‖Tt​f‖Lq​(γ)≤‖f‖Lp​(γ)\|T_{t}f\|_{L^{q}(\gamma)}\leq\|f\|_{L^{p}(\gamma)} (17)

for all f∈Lp​(γ)f\in L^{p}(\gamma) [21, 14]. A direct consequence for chaos components is the moment comparison inequality: for every g∈𝒞ng\in\mathcal{C}_{n} and q≥2q\geq 2,

‖g‖Lq​(γ)≤(q−1)n/2​‖g‖L2​(γ).\|g\|_{L^{q}(\gamma)}\leq(q-1)^{n/2}\,\|g\|_{L^{2}(\gamma)}. (18)

This follows by applying (17) with p=2p=2 and ρ=e−t=(q−1)−1/2\rho=e^{-t}=(q-1)^{-1/2} to g∈𝒞ng\in\mathcal{C}_{n}, using Tt​g=e−n​t​gT_{t}g=e^{-nt}g [14, Corollary 5.11]. Equation (18) bounds the higher moments of a fixed chaos component; the exponential decay of chaos coefficients with order nn requires additional regularity and is established separately in Theorem 2 via a Cauchy-estimate argument.

Gauss–Hermite quadrature.

To evaluate integrals against γ\gamma numerically, we use Gauss–Hermite quadrature [11, 37]. An SS-point rule {(ωs,μs)}s=1S\{(\omega_{s},\mu_{s})\}_{s=1}^{S} approximates

∫ℝf⁡(ω)​𝑑γ​(ω)≈∑s=1Sμs​f​(ωs),\int_{\mathbb{R}}f(\omega)\,d\gamma(\omega)\;\approx\;\sum_{s=1}^{S}\mu_{s}\,f(\omega_{s}), (19)

where the nodes ω1<⋯<ωS\omega_{1}<\cdots<\omega_{S} are the roots of HeS​(ω)\mathrm{He}_{S}(\omega) and the weights μs>0\mu_{s}>0 sum to one. The main property is polynomial exactness: the approximation is exact whenever ff is a polynomial of degree at most 2​S−12S-1 [32]. In particular:

  • •

    Orthonormality: ∑s=1Sμs​Ψm​(ωs)​Ψn​(ωs)=δm​n\sum_{s=1}^{S}\mu_{s}\,\Psi_{m}(\omega_{s})\,\Psi_{n}(\omega_{s})=\delta_{mn} for all m+n≤2​S−1m+n\leq 2S-1.

  • •

    Triple products: ∑s=1Sμs​Ψr​(ωs)​Ψn​(ωs)​Ψm​(ωs)=𝔼⁡[Ψr​Ψn​Ψm]\sum_{s=1}^{S}\mu_{s}\,\Psi_{r}(\omega_{s})\Psi_{n}(\omega_{s})\Psi_{m}(\omega_{s})=\mathbb{E}[\Psi_{r}\Psi_{n}\Psi_{m}] whenever r+n+m≤2​S−1r+n+m\leq 2S-1.

For DSS-GNN with chaos order PP and gate order PgP_{g}, the most demanding integrand is the triple product Ψr​Ψn​Ψm\Psi_{r}\Psi_{n}\Psi_{m} with r≤Pgr\leq P_{g}, n,m≤Pn,m\leq P, which has degree Pg+2​PP_{g}+2P. Exactness therefore requires S≥⌈(Pg+2​P+1)/2⌉S\geq\lceil(P_{g}+2P+1)/2\rceil quadrature nodes. For Pg≤1P_{g}\leq 1 the threshold is S≥P+1S\geq P+1; the experiments use S=4S=4, which is exact for P≤3P\leq 3.

Remark 3 (Non-intrusive vs. intrusive projection).

In the polynomial chaos literature [37], two strategies compute the chaos coefficients of a transformed variable σ⁡(H⁡(ω))\sigma(H(\omega)): (i) intrusive methods analytically propagate the expansion through σ\sigma using triple-product coefficients (Lemma 1); (ii) non-intrusive methods evaluate σ\sigma at quadrature nodes and project back (19). DSS-GNN uses the non-intrusive approach (6) because it applies unchanged to any pointwise activation σ\sigma without requiring closed-form triple-product expansions. Theorem 3 proves exact agreement for product terms α⁡(ω)​H​(ω)\alpha(\omega)H(\omega) when the quadrature rule integrates the relevant triple products exactly; for a general nonlinear activation σ\sigma, the non-intrusive projection remains an approximation whose error is decomposed in Proposition 3.

A.2 Supporting technical results

Lemma 1 (Products in chaos: triple-product contraction).

Let α⁡(ω)=∑r=0Pgar​Ψr​(ω)\alpha(\omega)=\sum_{r=0}^{P_{g}}a_{r}\Psi_{r}(\omega) and H⁡(ω)=∑n=0PHn​Ψn​(ω)H(\omega)=\sum_{n=0}^{P}H_{n}\Psi_{n}(\omega). Then the order-mm coefficient of the product α⁡(ω)​H​(ω)\alpha(\omega)H(\omega) is

(α​H)m=∑r=0Pg∑n=0Par​Hn​cr​n​m,cr​n​m:=𝔼⁡[Ψr​Ψn​Ψm].(\alpha H)_{m}=\sum_{r=0}^{P_{g}}\sum_{n=0}^{P}a_{r}H_{n}\,c_{rnm},\qquad c_{rnm}:=\mathbb{E}[\Psi_{r}\Psi_{n}\Psi_{m}].
Proof.

Expand the product in the Hermite basis:

α⁡(ω)​H​(ω)=(∑r=0Pgar​Ψr​(ω))​(∑n=0PHn​Ψn​(ω))=∑r,nar​Hn​Ψr​(ω)​Ψn​(ω).\alpha(\omega)H(\omega)=\Bigl(\sum_{r=0}^{P_{g}}a_{r}\Psi_{r}(\omega)\Bigr)\Bigl(\sum_{n=0}^{P}H_{n}\Psi_{n}(\omega)\Bigr)=\sum_{r,n}a_{r}H_{n}\,\Psi_{r}(\omega)\Psi_{n}(\omega).

The order-mm coefficient is obtained by projecting onto Ψm\Psi_{m} using the orthonormality 𝔼⁡[Ψi​Ψj]=δi​j\mathbb{E}[\Psi_{i}\Psi_{j}]=\delta_{ij}:

(α​H)m=𝔼⁡[α⁡(ω)​H​(ω)​Ψm​(ω)]=∑r,nar​Hn​𝔼​[Ψr​Ψn​Ψm]=∑r,nar​Hn​cr​n​m.(\alpha H)_{m}=\mathbb{E}\bigl[\alpha(\omega)H(\omega)\Psi_{m}(\omega)\bigr]=\sum_{r,n}a_{r}H_{n}\,\mathbb{E}[\Psi_{r}\Psi_{n}\Psi_{m}]=\sum_{r,n}a_{r}H_{n}\,c_{rnm}.

The triple-product constants cr​n​m=𝔼⁡[Ψr​Ψn​Ψm]c_{rnm}=\mathbb{E}[\Psi_{r}\Psi_{n}\Psi_{m}] are computable in closed form from the three-term recurrence of the probabilists’ Hermite polynomials [37]. In particular, cr​n​m=0c_{rnm}=0 unless |r−n|≤m≤r+n|r-n|\leq m\leq r+n and r+n+mr+n+m is even, which makes the coupling matrices sparse. ∎

Theorem 3 (Non-intrusive projection recovers product coefficients when quadrature is exact).

Let (α​H)^m:=∑s=1Sμs​α​(ωs)​H​(ωs)​Ψm​(ωs)\widehat{(\alpha H)}_{m}:=\sum_{s=1}^{S}\mu_{s}\,\alpha(\omega_{s})H(\omega_{s})\Psi_{m}(\omega_{s}) be the discrete projection of the product using a Gauss–Hermite quadrature rule {(ωs,μs)}s=1S\{(\omega_{s},\mu_{s})\}_{s=1}^{S}. If the quadrature integrates all triple products Ψr​(ω)​Ψn​(ω)​Ψm​(ω)\Psi_{r}(\omega)\Psi_{n}(\omega)\Psi_{m}(\omega) exactly for r≤Pgr\leq P_{g}, n≤Pn\leq P, m≤Pm\leq P, then (α​H)^m=(α​H)m\widehat{(\alpha H)}_{m}=(\alpha H)_{m} for all m≤Pm\leq P.

Proof.

Substituting the expansions of α\alpha and HH:

(α​H)^m\displaystyle\widehat{(\alpha H)}_{m} =∑s=1Sμs​α​(ωs)​H​(ωs)​Ψm​(ωs)\displaystyle=\sum_{s=1}^{S}\mu_{s}\,\alpha(\omega_{s})H(\omega_{s})\Psi_{m}(\omega_{s})
=∑s=1Sμs​∑r=0Pg∑n=0Par​Hn​Ψr​(ωs)​Ψn​(ωs)​Ψm​(ωs)\displaystyle=\sum_{s=1}^{S}\mu_{s}\sum_{r=0}^{P_{g}}\sum_{n=0}^{P}a_{r}H_{n}\,\Psi_{r}(\omega_{s})\Psi_{n}(\omega_{s})\Psi_{m}(\omega_{s})
=∑r,nar​Hn​∑s=1Sμs​Ψr​(ωs)​Ψn​(ωs)​Ψm​(ωs)⏟QS​[Ψr​Ψn​Ψm].\displaystyle=\sum_{r,n}a_{r}H_{n}\underbrace{\sum_{s=1}^{S}\mu_{s}\,\Psi_{r}(\omega_{s})\Psi_{n}(\omega_{s})\Psi_{m}(\omega_{s})}_{\displaystyle Q_{S}[\Psi_{r}\Psi_{n}\Psi_{m}]}.

The integrand Ψr​Ψn​Ψm\Psi_{r}\Psi_{n}\Psi_{m} is a polynomial of degree r+n+m≤Pg+2​Pr+n+m\leq P_{g}+2P under the Gaussian weight γ\gamma. An SS-point Gauss–Hermite rule integrates polynomials of degree up to 2​S−12S-1 exactly [37]. The condition 2​S−1≥Pg+2​P2S-1\geq P_{g}+2P, i.e. S≥⌈(Pg+2​P+1)/2⌉S\geq\lceil(P_{g}+2P+1)/2\rceil, therefore ensures QS​[Ψr​Ψn​Ψm]=𝔼⁡[Ψr​Ψn​Ψm]=cr​n​mQ_{S}[\Psi_{r}\Psi_{n}\Psi_{m}]=\mathbb{E}[\Psi_{r}\Psi_{n}\Psi_{m}]=c_{rnm}. By Lemma 1, (α​H)^m=(α​H)m\widehat{(\alpha H)}_{m}=(\alpha H)_{m}. ∎

Proposition 3 (Discrete projection error decomposition).

Let ΠP\Pi_{P} be the exact L2​(ℝ,γ)L^{2}(\mathbb{R},\gamma) projection onto the first P+1P+1 Wiener chaos orders, and let ΠP,S​Q\Pi_{P,S}Q be the finite chaos expansion whose coefficients are induced by a quadrature rule: (ΠP,S​Q)m:=∑s=1Sμs​Q​(ωs)​Ψm​(ωs)(\Pi_{P,S}Q)_{m}:=\sum_{s=1}^{S}\mu_{s}\,Q(\omega_{s})\Psi_{m}(\omega_{s}). Then for any Q∈L2​(ℝ,γ)Q\in L^{2}(\mathbb{R},\gamma),

‖Q−ΠP,S​Q‖L2≤‖Q−ΠP​Q‖L2⏟truncation error+‖ΠP​Q−ΠP,S​Q‖L2⏟quadrature error.\|Q-\Pi_{P,S}Q\|_{L^{2}}\;\leq\;\underbrace{\|Q-\Pi_{P}Q\|_{L^{2}}}_{\text{truncation error}}+\underbrace{\|\Pi_{P}Q-\Pi_{P,S}Q\|_{L^{2}}}_{\text{quadrature error}}.

Moreover, Gauss–Hermite rules yield exact coefficients whenever Q⁡(ω)​Ψm​(ω)Q(\omega)\Psi_{m}(\omega) is a polynomial of sufficiently low degree under the Gaussian weight.

Proof.

The triangle inequality in L2​(ℝ,γ)L^{2}(\mathbb{R},\gamma) gives ‖Q−ΠP,S​Q‖≤‖Q−ΠP​Q‖+‖ΠP​Q−ΠP,S​Q‖\|Q-\Pi_{P,S}Q\|\leq\|Q-\Pi_{P}Q\|+\|\Pi_{P}Q-\Pi_{P,S}Q\|. For the truncation term, ΠP\Pi_{P} is the orthogonal projection onto ⨁n=0P𝒞n\bigoplus_{n=0}^{P}\mathcal{C}_{n}, the direct sum of the first P+1P+1 Wiener chaos subspaces [14], so ‖Q−ΠP​Q‖2=∑n>P‖Qn‖2\|Q-\Pi_{P}Q\|^{2}=\sum_{n>P}\|Q_{n}\|^{2} where Qn=𝔼⁡[Q​Ψn]Q_{n}=\mathbb{E}[Q\Psi_{n}] are the exact chaos coefficients. For the quadrature term, the mm-th coefficient of ΠP,S​Q\Pi_{P,S}Q is ∑sμs​Q​(ωs)​Ψm​(ωs)\sum_{s}\mu_{s}Q(\omega_{s})\Psi_{m}(\omega_{s}), which approximates ∫Q​Ψm​𝑑γ\int Q\Psi_{m}\,d\gamma. When Q​ΨmQ\Psi_{m} is a polynomial of degree at most 2​S−12S-1, Gauss–Hermite quadrature integrates it exactly [37], making the quadrature error zero. In the DSS layer context, the pre-activation H~(ℓ+1)​(ω)\widetilde{H}^{(\ell+1)}(\omega) before applying σ\sigma is a polynomial of degree at most Pg+PP_{g}+P in ω\omega; after applying σ\sigma it is no longer polynomial, and the quadrature error reflects the approximation quality of the SS-point rule on this non-polynomial integrand. ∎

A.3 Proof of Proposition 1 (Generalization)

See 1

Proof.

When P=0P=0, the chaos expansion (2) contains a single term: H(ℓ)​(ω)=H0(ℓ)​Ψ0​(ω)H^{(\ell)}(\omega)=H_{0}^{(\ell)}\Psi_{0}(\omega). Since the zeroth normalized Hermite polynomial satisfies Ψ0≡1\Psi_{0}\equiv 1 [37], the representation is deterministic: H(ℓ)​(ω)=H0(ℓ)H^{(\ell)}(\omega)=H_{0}^{(\ell)} for all ω∈Ω\omega\in\Omega.

Step 1 (Gate reduction). With P=0P=0, the mixing weights (4) are indexed by n=0n=0 only. Setting the gate order Pg=0P_{g}=0 (no stochastic gating when the representation itself is deterministic) yields scalar constants α0=a0,0∈ℝ\alpha_{0}=a_{0,0}\in\mathbb{R} and β0=b0,0∈ℝ\beta_{0}=b_{0,0}\in\mathbb{R}.

Step 2 (Pre-activation collapse). The quadrature-node pre-activation (5) reduces to

H~(ℓ+1)​(ωs)\displaystyle\widetilde{H}^{(\ell+1)}(\omega_{s}) =Ψ0​(ωs)​(α0​Glp​(LG)​H0(ℓ)+β0​Ghp​(LG)​H0(ℓ))​Wℓ\displaystyle=\Psi_{0}(\omega_{s})\bigl(\alpha_{0}\,G_{\mathrm{lp}}(L_{G})H_{0}^{(\ell)}+\beta_{0}\,G_{\mathrm{hp}}(L_{G})H_{0}^{(\ell)}\bigr)W_{\ell}
=(α0​Glp​(LG)+β0​Ghp​(LG))​H0(ℓ)​Wℓ,\displaystyle=\bigl(\alpha_{0}\,G_{\mathrm{lp}}(L_{G})+\beta_{0}\,G_{\mathrm{hp}}(L_{G})\bigr)H_{0}^{(\ell)}W_{\ell},

which is independent of the quadrature node ωs\omega_{s}.

Step 3 (Projection collapse). The projection (6) for m=0m=0 becomes

H0(ℓ+1)=∑s=1Sμs​σ​(H~(ℓ+1)​(ωs))​Ψ0​(ωs)=σ⁡(H~(ℓ+1))​∑s=1Sμs=σ⁡(H~(ℓ+1)),H_{0}^{(\ell+1)}=\sum_{s=1}^{S}\mu_{s}\,\sigma\!\bigl(\widetilde{H}^{(\ell+1)}(\omega_{s})\bigr)\Psi_{0}(\omega_{s})=\sigma\!\bigl(\widetilde{H}^{(\ell+1)}\bigr)\sum_{s=1}^{S}\mu_{s}=\sigma\!\bigl(\widetilde{H}^{(\ell+1)}\bigr),

where the second equality uses the fact that H~(ℓ+1)\widetilde{H}^{(\ell+1)} does not depend on ωs\omega_{s} (Step 2), and the third uses the normalization ∑sμs=∫ℝ𝑑γ=1\sum_{s}\mu_{s}=\int_{\mathbb{R}}d\gamma=1 of the Gauss–Hermite weights [37].

Step 4 (Recovery of spectral GNN). Combining Steps 2 and 3, the full DSS layer update at P=0P=0 is

H0(ℓ+1)=σ⁡(g⁡(LG)​H0(ℓ)​Wℓ),g⁡(LG):=α0​Glp​(LG)+β0​Ghp​(LG).H_{0}^{(\ell+1)}=\sigma\!\bigl(g(L_{G})\,H_{0}^{(\ell)}\,W_{\ell}\bigr),\qquad g(L_{G}):=\alpha_{0}\,G_{\mathrm{lp}}(L_{G})+\beta_{0}\,G_{\mathrm{hp}}(L_{G}).

Since GlpG_{\mathrm{lp}} and GhpG_{\mathrm{hp}} are Chebyshev polynomials in LGL_{G} (3), their linear combination g⁡(LG)g(L_{G}) is a polynomial in LGL_{G} of degree max⁡(Klp,Khp)\max(K_{\mathrm{lp}},K_{\mathrm{hp}}). This is exactly the form of a polynomial spectral graph convolution layer [6, 29]: the filter gg acts in the graph-frequency domain as g⁡(λj)=α0​glp​(λj)+β0​ghp​(λj)g(\lambda_{j})=\alpha_{0}\,g_{\mathrm{lp}}(\lambda_{j})+\beta_{0}\,g_{\mathrm{hp}}(\lambda_{j}), where glp​(λ)=∑kck(lp)​Tk​(λ~)g_{\mathrm{lp}}(\lambda)=\sum_{k}c_{k}^{(\mathrm{lp})}T_{k}(\tilde{\lambda}) is the scalar frequency response of the low-pass branch and λ~=2​λ/λmax−1\tilde{\lambda}=2\lambda/\lambda_{\max}-1.

Special cases. Setting β0=0\beta_{0}=0 and Klp=1K_{\mathrm{lp}}=1 with the renormalization trick of Kipf and Welling [15] yields GCN as a single-layer DSS-GNN with P=0P=0. Allowing arbitrary Chebyshev degree with both filter branches active recovers ChebNet [6] in its scalar-coefficient form (filter weights Θk=ck​Wℓ\Theta_{k}=c_{k}W_{\ell}). With generalized polynomial coefficient learning, GPR-GNN [5] and BernNet [13] are similarly obtained as P=0P=0 specializations. ∎

A.4 Proof of Theorem 1 (Doubly-spectral operator)

Lemma 2 (Exact-projection conditions for the joint transfer).

In Theorem 1, assume the pointwise nonlinearity is omitted, the gates have chaos degree at most PgP_{g}, the state has chaos degree at most PP, and the Gauss–Hermite rule integrates all triple products Ψr​Ψn​Ψm\Psi_{r}\Psi_{n}\Psi_{m} with r≤Pgr\leq P_{g} and n,m≤Pn,m\leq P. A sufficient condition is S≥⌈(Pg+2​P+1)/2⌉S\geq\lceil(P_{g}+2P+1)/2\rceil. Under this condition, the stochastic coupling matrices in the joint-transfer formula are

Mm​n(ℓ,lp):=∑r=0Pgan,r​cr​n​m,Mm​n(ℓ,hp):=∑r=0Pgbn,r​cr​n​m,cr​n​m:=𝔼⁡[Ψr​Ψn​Ψm].M_{mn}^{(\ell,\mathrm{lp})}:=\sum_{r=0}^{P_{g}}a_{n,r}\,c_{rnm},\qquad M_{mn}^{(\ell,\mathrm{hp})}:=\sum_{r=0}^{P_{g}}b_{n,r}\,c_{rnm},\qquad c_{rnm}:=\mathbb{E}[\Psi_{r}\Psi_{n}\Psi_{m}].
Proof.

The product Ψr​Ψn​Ψm\Psi_{r}\Psi_{n}\Psi_{m} has degree at most Pg+2​PP_{g}+2P under the stated index ranges. An SS-point Gauss–Hermite rule is exact for polynomials of degree at most 2​S−12S-1, so 2​S−1≥Pg+2​P2S-1\geq P_{g}+2P suffices. The coupling matrix definitions are obtained by collecting the exactly projected triple-product coefficients in the linearized DSS update. ∎

See 1

Proof.

Let {uj}j=1N\{u_{j}\}_{j=1}^{N} be the orthonormal eigenvectors of the graph Laplacian LGL_{G} with eigenvalues {λj}j=1N\{\lambda_{j}\}_{j=1}^{N}, so that LG=∑j=1Nλj​uj​uj⊤L_{G}=\sum_{j=1}^{N}\lambda_{j}\,u_{j}u_{j}^{\top} [29]. Because the Chebyshev filters (3) are polynomials in LGL_{G}, each eigenvector is simultaneously an eigenvector of both filters:

Glp​(LG)​uj=glp​(λj)​uj,Ghp​(LG)​uj=ghp​(λj)​uj,G_{\mathrm{lp}}(L_{G})\,u_{j}=g_{\mathrm{lp}}(\lambda_{j})\,u_{j},\qquad G_{\mathrm{hp}}(L_{G})\,u_{j}=g_{\mathrm{hp}}(\lambda_{j})\,u_{j}, (20)

where glp​(λ)=∑kck(lp)​Tk​(λ~)g_{\mathrm{lp}}(\lambda)=\sum_{k}c_{k}^{(\mathrm{lp})}T_{k}(\tilde{\lambda}) and ghp​(λ)=∑kck(hp)​Tk​(λ~)g_{\mathrm{hp}}(\lambda)=\sum_{k}c_{k}^{(\mathrm{hp})}T_{k}(\tilde{\lambda}) are the scalar frequency responses.

Step 1 (Graph Fourier transform of chaos coefficients). Define the joint spectral coefficient at graph frequency λj\lambda_{j} and chaos order nn as H^n(ℓ)​(λj):=uj⊤​Hn(ℓ)∈ℝ1×dℓ\hat{H}_{n}^{(\ell)}(\lambda_{j}):=u_{j}^{\top}H_{n}^{(\ell)}\in\mathbb{R}^{1\times d_{\ell}}. For proof convenience, write Unlp:=Glp​(LG)​Hn(ℓ)U_{n}^{\mathrm{lp}}:=G_{\mathrm{lp}}(L_{G})H_{n}^{(\ell)} and Unhp:=Ghp​(LG)​Hn(ℓ)U_{n}^{\mathrm{hp}}:=G_{\mathrm{hp}}(L_{G})H_{n}^{(\ell)}. These spectrally filtered coefficients from (5) satisfy

uj⊤​Unlp=uj⊤​Glp​(LG)​Hn(ℓ)=glp​(λj)​H^n(ℓ)​(λj),u_{j}^{\top}U_{n}^{\mathrm{lp}}=u_{j}^{\top}G_{\mathrm{lp}}(L_{G})\,H_{n}^{(\ell)}=g_{\mathrm{lp}}(\lambda_{j})\;\hat{H}_{n}^{(\ell)}(\lambda_{j}), (21)

and analogously uj⊤​Unhp=ghp​(λj)​H^n(ℓ)​(λj)u_{j}^{\top}U_{n}^{\mathrm{hp}}=g_{\mathrm{hp}}(\lambda_{j})\;\hat{H}_{n}^{(\ell)}(\lambda_{j}).

Step 2 (Linearized update in the chaos basis). Omitting the pointwise nonlinearity σ\sigma (linearization), the DSS update (5)–(6) gives

Hm(ℓ+1)\displaystyle H_{m}^{(\ell+1)} =∑s=1Sμs​H~(ℓ+1)​(ωs)​Ψm​(ωs)\displaystyle=\sum_{s=1}^{S}\mu_{s}\,\widetilde{H}^{(\ell+1)}(\omega_{s})\,\Psi_{m}(\omega_{s})
=∑s=1Sμs​∑n=0PΨn​(ωs)​(αn​(ωs)​Unlp+βn​(ωs)​Unhp)​Wℓ​Ψm​(ωs).\displaystyle=\sum_{s=1}^{S}\mu_{s}\sum_{n=0}^{P}\Psi_{n}(\omega_{s})\bigl(\alpha_{n}(\omega_{s})\,U_{n}^{\mathrm{lp}}+\beta_{n}(\omega_{s})\,U_{n}^{\mathrm{hp}}\bigr)W_{\ell}\;\Psi_{m}(\omega_{s}). (22)

Expanding the gates αn​(ωs)=∑r=0Pgan,r​Ψr​(ωs)\alpha_{n}(\omega_{s})=\sum_{r=0}^{P_{g}}a_{n,r}\Psi_{r}(\omega_{s}) from (4) and exchanging the order of summation:

Hm(ℓ+1)\displaystyle H_{m}^{(\ell+1)} =∑n=0P[(∑r=0Pgan,r∑s=1Sμs​Ψr​(ωs)​Ψn​(ωs)​Ψm​(ωs)⏟=cr​n​m)Unlp\displaystyle=\sum_{n=0}^{P}\Bigl[\Bigl(\sum_{r=0}^{P_{g}}a_{n,r}\underbrace{\sum_{s=1}^{S}\mu_{s}\,\Psi_{r}(\omega_{s})\Psi_{n}(\omega_{s})\Psi_{m}(\omega_{s})}_{=\;c_{rnm}}\Bigr)U_{n}^{\mathrm{lp}}
+(∑r=0Pgbn,rcr​n​m)Unhp]Wℓ,\displaystyle\quad\;+\Bigl(\sum_{r=0}^{P_{g}}b_{n,r}\,c_{rnm}\Bigr)U_{n}^{\mathrm{hp}}\Bigr]W_{\ell}, (23)

where the identification ∑sμs​Ψr​(ωs)​Ψn​(ωs)​Ψm​(ωs)=cr​n​m:=𝔼⁡[Ψr​Ψn​Ψm]\sum_{s}\mu_{s}\,\Psi_{r}(\omega_{s})\Psi_{n}(\omega_{s})\Psi_{m}(\omega_{s})=c_{rnm}:=\mathbb{E}[\Psi_{r}\Psi_{n}\Psi_{m}] follows from Theorem 3: the Gauss–Hermite rule integrates the triple product exactly when SS is sufficiently large.

Define the chaos coupling matrices M(ℓ,lp),M(ℓ,hp)∈ℝ(P+1)×(P+1)M^{(\ell,\mathrm{lp})},\,M^{(\ell,\mathrm{hp})}\in\mathbb{R}^{(P+1)\times(P+1)} with entries

Mm​n(ℓ,lp):=∑r=0Pgan,r​cr​n​m,Mm​n(ℓ,hp):=∑r=0Pgbn,r​cr​n​m.M_{mn}^{(\ell,\mathrm{lp})}:=\sum_{r=0}^{P_{g}}a_{n,r}\,c_{rnm},\qquad M_{mn}^{(\ell,\mathrm{hp})}:=\sum_{r=0}^{P_{g}}b_{n,r}\,c_{rnm}. (24)

Then (23) simplifies to

Hm(ℓ+1)=∑n=0P(Mm​n(ℓ,lp)​Unlp+Mm​n(ℓ,hp)​Unhp)​Wℓ.H_{m}^{(\ell+1)}=\sum_{n=0}^{P}\bigl(M_{mn}^{(\ell,\mathrm{lp})}\,U_{n}^{\mathrm{lp}}+M_{mn}^{(\ell,\mathrm{hp})}\,U_{n}^{\mathrm{hp}}\bigr)\,W_{\ell}. (25)

Step 3 (Joint spectral representation). Left-multiplying (25) by uj⊤u_{j}^{\top} and applying (21):

H^m(ℓ+1)​(λj)=∑n=0P(Mm​n(ℓ,lp)​glp​(λj)+Mm​n(ℓ,hp)​ghp​(λj))​H^n(ℓ)​(λj)​Wℓ.\hat{H}_{m}^{(\ell+1)}(\lambda_{j})=\sum_{n=0}^{P}\bigl(M_{mn}^{(\ell,\mathrm{lp})}\,g_{\mathrm{lp}}(\lambda_{j})+M_{mn}^{(\ell,\mathrm{hp})}\,g_{\mathrm{hp}}(\lambda_{j})\bigr)\;\hat{H}_{n}^{(\ell)}(\lambda_{j})\;W_{\ell}.

Stack the chaos orders into a matrix 𝐇^(ℓ)​(λj):=[H^0(ℓ)​(λj);…;H^P(ℓ)​(λj)]∈ℝ(P+1)×dℓ\widehat{\mathbf{H}}^{(\ell)}(\lambda_{j}):=\bigl[\hat{H}_{0}^{(\ell)}(\lambda_{j});\;\ldots\;;\;\hat{H}_{P}^{(\ell)}(\lambda_{j})\bigr]\in\mathbb{R}^{(P+1)\times d_{\ell}}. The equation above is the (m,⋅)(m,\cdot) row of the matrix relation

𝐇^(ℓ+1)​(λj)=ℋ(ℓ)​(λj)​𝐇^(ℓ)​(λj)​Wℓ,\widehat{\mathbf{H}}^{(\ell+1)}(\lambda_{j})=\mathcal{H}^{(\ell)}(\lambda_{j})\;\widehat{\mathbf{H}}^{(\ell)}(\lambda_{j})\;W_{\ell}, (26)

where the (P+1)×(P+1)(P{+}1)\times(P{+}1) transfer matrix decomposes as

ℋ(ℓ)​(λ)=glp​(λ)​M(ℓ,lp)+ghp​(λ)​M(ℓ,hp).\mathcal{H}^{(\ell)}(\lambda)=g_{\mathrm{lp}}(\lambda)\;M^{(\ell,\mathrm{lp})}+g_{\mathrm{hp}}(\lambda)\;M^{(\ell,\mathrm{hp})}. (27)

Interpretation. Equation (26) shows that, in the linearized regime, the DSS layer implements a learned linear operator on the joint spectral domain of the doubly-spectral expansion (1). The decomposition (27) separates two independent mechanisms:

  1. 1.

    Graph-frequency response: the scalar functions glp​(λ)g_{\mathrm{lp}}(\lambda) and ghp​(λ)g_{\mathrm{hp}}(\lambda) shape how the layer responds to each graph eigenvalue λj\lambda_{j}, exactly as in standard spectral GNNs [6, 29].

  2. 2.

    Chaos-order coupling: the matrices M(ℓ,lp)M^{(\ell,\mathrm{lp})} and M(ℓ,hp)M^{(\ell,\mathrm{hp})} control the coupling between chaos orders 0,…,P0,\ldots,P, enabling the layer to redistribute energy across the chaos spectrum.

Together, these two axes parameterize a bilinear family of operators on the tensor-product Hilbert space ℓ2​(V)⊗L2​(ℝ,γ)\ell^{2}(V)\otimes L^{2}(\mathbb{R},\gamma), thereby justifying the doubly-spectral designation. ∎

A.5 Proof of Theorem 2 (Representational capacity and truncation)

See 2

Proof of the approximation claim.

The proof proceeds in three stages: (i) truncation in the chaos-order axis, (ii) a rank argument for the quadrature projection, and (iii) a one-layer constructive realization using the final linear readout.

Step 1 (Chaos-order truncation). By the Wiener–Itô chaos decomposition [14], any Y∈L2​(ℝ,γ,ℝN×d)Y\in L^{2}(\mathbb{R},\gamma;\mathbb{R}^{N\times d}) admits the expansion Y⁡(ω)=∑n=0∞Yn​Ψn​(ω)Y(\omega)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}Y_{n}\Psi_{n}(\omega) with deterministic coefficients Yn=𝔼⁡[Y​Ψn]∈ℝN×dY_{n}=\mathbb{E}[Y\Psi_{n}]\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times d}, and by Parseval’s identity ‖Y‖L22=∑n=0∞‖Yn‖F2<∞\|Y\|_{L^{2}}^{2}=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\|Y_{n}\|_{F}^{2}<\infty. Fix a truncation order PP for the construction. For the density claim, fix ε>0\varepsilon>0 and take this PP large enough that ∑n>P‖Yn‖F2<ε2\sum_{n>P}\|Y_{n}\|_{F}^{2}<\varepsilon^{2}; for the explicit rate, keep PP arbitrary and apply the tail estimate proved below.

Step 2 (Quadrature projection rank). Take S=P+1S=P+1 and let {(ωs,μs)}s=1S\{(\omega_{s},\mu_{s})\}_{s=1}^{S} be the associated SS-point Gauss–Hermite rule. Define the projection matrix Φ∈ℝ(P+1)×S\Phi\in\mathbb{R}^{(P+1)\times S} with entries Φn​s=μs​Ψn​(ωs)\Phi_{ns}=\mu_{s}\,\Psi_{n}(\omega_{s}). The Hermite polynomials Ψ0,…,ΨP\Psi_{0},\ldots,\Psi_{P} are linearly independent on the S=P+1S=P+1 distinct quadrature nodes, and μs>0\mu_{s}>0 for all ss, so Φ\Phi is invertible. Consequently, for any target coefficients {Yn}n=0P\{Y_{n}\}_{n=0}^{P}, there exist matrices {Vs}s=1S\{V_{s}\}_{s=1}^{S} in ℝN×d\mathbb{R}^{N\times d} satisfying

∑s=1SμsVsΨn(ωs)=Yn,n=0,…,P.\sum_{s=1}^{S}\mu_{s}\,V_{s}\,\Psi_{n}(\omega_{s})=Y_{n},\qquad n=0,\ldots,P. (28)

Step 3 (Constructive one-layer realization with ReLU). We construct a one-layer DSS-GNN (L=1L=1) whose post-readout output matches the truncated coefficients exactly. Let q:=2​dq:=2d and define the nonnegative hidden targets

Rs:=[Vs+,Vs−]∈ℝ+N×q,Vs=Vs+−Vs−,R_{s}:=[V_{s}^{+},\,V_{s}^{-}]\in\mathbb{R}_{+}^{N\times q},\qquad V_{s}=V_{s}^{+}-V_{s}^{-},

where Vs+,Vs−V_{s}^{+},V_{s}^{-} are the entrywise positive and negative parts of VsV_{s}. Choose the final readout

Wout=[Id−Id]∈ℝq×d,W_{\mathrm{out}}=\begin{bmatrix}I_{d}\\[2.0pt] -I_{d}\end{bmatrix}\in\mathbb{R}^{q\times d},

so that Rs​Wout=VsR_{s}W_{\mathrm{out}}=V_{s} for every ss.

Next define the generalized Vandermonde matrix

Θ∈ℝS×S,Θs​t:=Ψt−1(ωs),s,t=1,…,S.\Theta\in\mathbb{R}^{S\times S},\qquad\Theta_{st}:=\Psi_{t-1}(\omega_{s}),\qquad s,t=1,\ldots,S.

Because Ψ0,…,ΨS−1\Psi_{0},\ldots,\Psi_{S-1} are linearly independent and the quadrature nodes ω1,…,ωS\omega_{1},\ldots,\omega_{S} are distinct, Θ\Theta is invertible. Hence for the prescribed matrices RsR_{s} there exist unique matrices A1,…,AS∈ℝN×qA_{1},\ldots,A_{S}\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times q} such that

∑t=1SΨt−1(ωs)At=Rs,s=1,…,S.\sum_{t=1}^{S}\Psi_{t-1}(\omega_{s})\,A_{t}=R_{s},\qquad s=1,\ldots,S. (29)

Next, we realize these AtA_{t} with the DSS layer. Set the lifted input width to d0=S​qd_{0}=Sq and partition the lifted features into SS blocks b1,…,bSb_{1},\ldots,b_{S}, each of width qq. Choose the graph filters and gates as

Glp​(LG)=I(Klp=0,c0(lp)=1),Ghp​(LG)=0,G_{\mathrm{lp}}(L_{G})=I\quad(K_{\mathrm{lp}}=0,\;c_{0}^{(\mathrm{lp})}=1),\qquad G_{\mathrm{hp}}(L_{G})=0,
αn​(ω)≡1​(n=0,…,P),βn​(ω)≡0,\alpha_{n}(\omega)\equiv 1\;\;(n=0,\ldots,P),\qquad\beta_{n}(\omega)\equiv 0,

so Pg=0P_{g}=0 suffices. Since rank⁡(X)=N\operatorname{rank}(X)=N, for each t=1,…,St=1,\ldots,S there exists a matrix Bt∈ℝdin×qB_{t}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\rm in}\times q} with X​Bt=AtXB_{t}=A_{t}. Set Win(t−1)W_{\mathrm{in}}^{(t-1)} to place BtB_{t} in block btb_{t} and zeros elsewhere. Then Ht−1(0)=X​Win(t−1)H_{t-1}^{(0)}=XW_{\mathrm{in}}^{(t-1)} is zero outside block btb_{t} and equals AtA_{t} on block btb_{t}.

Finally, choose W0∈ℝd0×qW_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{0}\times q} so that each row-block corresponding to btb_{t} equals the identity IqI_{q}. At quadrature node ωs\omega_{s}, the quadrature-node pre-activation becomes

H~(1)​(ωs)=∑t=1SΨt−1​(ωs)​At=Rs\widetilde{H}^{(1)}(\omega_{s})=\sum_{t=1}^{S}\Psi_{t-1}(\omega_{s})\,A_{t}=R_{s}

by (29). Since each RsR_{s} is entrywise nonnegative and σ=ReLU\sigma=\mathrm{ReLU}, we obtain

σ⁡(H~(1)​(ωs))=Rs,σ⁡(H~(1)​(ωs))​Wout=Vs.\sigma\!\bigl(\widetilde{H}^{(1)}(\omega_{s})\bigr)=R_{s},\qquad\sigma\!\bigl(\widetilde{H}^{(1)}(\omega_{s})\bigr)W_{\mathrm{out}}=V_{s}.

Projecting back to chaos coefficients gives, for every m=0,…,Pm=0,\ldots,P,

Hm(1)​Wout=∑s=1Sμs​σ​(H~(1)​(ωs))​Wout​Ψm​(ωs)=∑s=1Sμs​Vs​Ψm​(ωs)=Ym,H_{m}^{(1)}W_{\mathrm{out}}=\sum_{s=1}^{S}\mu_{s}\,\sigma\!\bigl(\widetilde{H}^{(1)}(\omega_{s})\bigr)W_{\mathrm{out}}\Psi_{m}(\omega_{s})=\sum_{s=1}^{S}\mu_{s}\,V_{s}\,\Psi_{m}(\omega_{s})=Y_{m},

where the last equality is exactly (28).

Step 4 (Combining with the tail). The retained coefficients are matched exactly, so the order-PP output Y~P\widetilde{Y}_{P} lies in ⨁n=0P𝒞n⊗ℝN×d\bigoplus_{n=0}^{P}\mathcal{C}_{n}\otimes\mathbb{R}^{N\times d} and has no chaos coefficients for n>Pn>P. By orthogonality of the chaos subspaces and Parseval’s identity, it satisfies

‖Y−Y~P‖L22=∑n>P‖Yn‖F2.\|Y-\widetilde{Y}_{P}\|_{L^{2}}^{2}=\sum_{n>P}\|Y_{n}\|_{F}^{2}.

Thus choosing PP so that the right-hand side is below ε2\varepsilon^{2} proves density in L2L^{2}. ∎

Remark 4 (Practical vs. theoretical capacity).

The constructive part of Theorem 2 is an existence result for a restricted subfamily of DSS-GNNs: the proof requires rank⁡(X)=N\operatorname{rank}(X)=N (i.e., din≥Nd_{\rm in}\geq N), a one-layer construction with lifted width d0=2​d​S=2​d​(P+1)d_{0}=2dS=2d(P+1) and output width d1=2​dd_{1}=2d, quadrature size S=P+1S=P+1, the ReLU activation, constant gates (Pg=0P_{g}=0), the identity low-pass filter, and a final linear readout that combines positive and negative hidden channels. The construction uses the identity low-pass filter and constant gates, so it bounds the capacity of the chaos axis alone; Theorem 1 describes the graph-frequency axis. The practical model differs from these conditions (dind_{\rm in} is typically smaller than NN, PP is small, and the filters are learned), so the theorem establishes representational capacity, while calibration, OOD detection, and robustness are established empirically. The explicit exponential bound adds that, for targets satisfying the entire-extension condition, a low truncation order should capture most of the gain, which is empirically consistent with the plateau at P=1​–​2P=1\text{--}2 observed in Figure 3(b).

Remark 5 (Rank-deficient features).

When rank⁡(X)=r<N\operatorname{rank}(X)=r<N, the same construction still matches every truncated target whose chaos-coefficient columns lie in range⁡(X)\operatorname{range}(X), under one positivity condition required by the ReLU step: the nonnegative quadrature-node evaluations Rs=[Vs+,Vs−]R_{s}=[V_{s}^{+},V_{s}^{-}] of Step 3 must themselves have columns in range⁡(X)\operatorname{range}(X), since At=X​BtA_{t}=XB_{t} forces every AtA_{t}, and hence every RsR_{s}, into that range. The condition is satisfiable, for example, by appending a constant feature column to XX: with Vs+:=Vs+c​ 11⊤V_{s}^{+}:=V_{s}+c\,\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^{\top} and Vs−:=c​ 11⊤V_{s}^{-}:=c\,\mathbf{1}\mathbf{1}^{\top} for c≥maxs⁡‖Vs‖maxc\geq\max_{s}\|V_{s}\|_{\max}, both parts are nonnegative and have columns in range⁡([X,𝟏])⊇range⁡(X)\operatorname{range}([X,\mathbf{1}])\supseteq\operatorname{range}(X), so every truncated target with columns in range⁡([X,𝟏])\operatorname{range}([X,\mathbf{1}]) is matched. We state exactly this matching property; no claim is made for targets whose coefficients are outside that range.

A.6 Proof of the Truncation Bound in Theorem 2

The analytic Gaussian-growth condition referenced in Theorem 2 is the following: each centered coordinate Y¯i​k​(ω):=Yi​k​(ω)−𝔼⁡[Yi​k]\bar{Y}_{ik}(\omega):=Y_{ik}(\omega)-\mathbb{E}[Y_{ik}] extends to an entire function satisfying |Y¯i​k​(z)|≤Ai​k​exp⁡(a​|z|2)|\bar{Y}_{ik}(z)|\leq A_{ik}\exp(a|z|^{2}) for some a∈(0,14)a\in(0,\tfrac{1}{4}) uniform in (i,k)(i,k), with ∑i,kAi​k2<∞\sum_{i,k}A_{ik}^{2}<\infty. Under this condition, set α:=2​a/(1−2​a)<1\alpha:=2a/(1-2a)<1; the proof yields the theorem for every β∈(α,1)\beta\in(\sqrt{\alpha},1), with CtrC_{\rm tr} depending on aa, β\beta, and ∑i,kAi​k2\sum_{i,k}A_{ik}^{2}.

Proof of the truncation bound.

We prove the bound coordinate-wise and sum. Fix a centered coordinate function g:=Y¯i​kg:=\bar{Y}_{ik} with chaos coefficients cn:=𝔼⁡[g⁡(ω)​Ψn​(ω)]c_{n}:=\mathbb{E}[g(\omega)\Psi_{n}(\omega)], so that g⁡(ω)=∑n=1∞cn​Ψn​(ω)g(\omega)=\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}c_{n}\Psi_{n}(\omega).

Step 1 (Hermite generating function). The generating function of the normalized Hermite polynomials [32] gives ∑n=0∞tnn!​Ψn​(ω)=exp⁡(t​ω−t2/2)\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{t^{n}}{\sqrt{n!}}\Psi_{n}(\omega)=\exp(t\omega-t^{2}/2). Multiplying by g⁡(ω)g(\omega) and taking the Gaussian expectation yields

ϕ⁡(s):=∑n=1∞cnn!​sn=𝔼⁡[g⁡(ω+s)]=∫ℝg⁡(x+s)​𝑑γ​(x),\phi(s)\;:=\;\sum_{n=1}^{\infty}\frac{c_{n}}{\sqrt{n!}}\,s^{n}\;=\;\mathbb{E}\!\big[g(\omega+s)\big]\;=\;\int_{\mathbb{R}}g(x+s)\,d\gamma(x), (30)

which is verified by expanding gg in the Hermite basis and using 𝔼⁡[Ψn​(ω)​exp⁡(s​ω−s2/2)]=sn/n!\mathbb{E}[\Psi_{n}(\omega)\exp(s\omega-s^{2}/2)]=s^{n}/\sqrt{n!}. The series defining ϕ\phi converges for every complex ss because |cn|≤‖g‖L2​(γ)|c_{n}|\leq\|g\|_{L^{2}(\gamma)}, so ϕ\phi is entire; the right-hand side is entire by the growth bound below and dominated convergence, and the two sides agree for real ss, hence for all s∈ℂs\in\mathbb{C}.

Step 2 (Growth bound on ϕ\phi). The hypothesis |g⁡(z)|≤A​exp⁡(a​|z|2)|g(z)|\leq A\exp(a|z|^{2}) with a<14a<\tfrac{1}{4} gives

|ϕ⁡(s)|\displaystyle|\phi(s)| ≤∫ℝA​exp⁡(a​|x+s|2)​𝑑γ​(x)=A​ea​|s|2​∫ℝexp⁡(a​x2+2​a​x​Re⁡(s))​𝑑γ​(x).\displaystyle\leq\int_{\mathbb{R}}A\,\exp\!\big(a|x+s|^{2}\big)\,d\gamma(x)=A\,e^{a|s|^{2}}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\exp\!\big(ax^{2}+2a\,x\operatorname{Re}(s)\big)\,d\gamma(x).

Completing the square in the exponent (a​x2+2​a​Re⁡(s)​x−x2/2=−(12−a)​x2+2​a​Re⁡(s)​xax^{2}+2a\operatorname{Re}(s)\,x-x^{2}/2=-({\tfrac{1}{2}}-a)x^{2}+2a\operatorname{Re}(s)\,x, which is a Gaussian integral convergent for a<12a<\tfrac{1}{2}) yields

|ϕ⁡(s)|≤A1−2​a​exp⁡(a1−2​a​|s|2).|\phi(s)|\;\leq\;\frac{A}{\sqrt{1-2a}}\;\exp\!\Big(\frac{a}{1-2a}\,|s|^{2}\Big).

Step 3 (Cauchy estimate and Stirling bound). Since ϕ\phi is entire, Cauchy’s inequality on the circle |s|=R|s|=R gives

|cn|n!≤R−n​sup|s|=R|ϕ⁡(s)|≤A1−2​a​R−n​ea′​R2,a′:=a1−2​a.\frac{|c_{n}|}{\sqrt{n!}}\;\leq\;R^{-n}\sup_{|s|=R}|\phi(s)|\;\leq\;\frac{A}{\sqrt{1-2a}}\;R^{-n}\,e^{a^{\prime}R^{2}},\qquad a^{\prime}:=\frac{a}{1-2a}.

Setting R=n/(2​a′)R=\sqrt{n/(2a^{\prime})} (the minimizer of −n​ln⁡R+a′​R2-n\ln R+a^{\prime}R^{2}):

|cn|≤A1−2​a​n!​(2​a′n)n/2​en/2.|c_{n}|\;\leq\;\frac{A}{\sqrt{1-2a}}\;\sqrt{n!}\;\Big(\frac{2a^{\prime}}{n}\Big)^{n/2}e^{n/2}.

By Stirling’s inequality n!≤e1/2​(2​π​n)1/4​(n/e)n/2\sqrt{n!}\leq e^{1/2}(2\pi n)^{1/4}(n/e)^{n/2}, the product (n/e)n/2​(2​a′/n)n/2​en/2(n/e)^{n/2}(2a^{\prime}/n)^{n/2}e^{n/2} simplifies to (2​a′)n/2(2a^{\prime})^{n/2}, giving

cn2≤A2​e​2​π​n1−2​a​(2​a′)n=A2​e​2​π​n1−2​a​αn,α:=2​a′=2​a1−2​a.c_{n}^{2}\;\leq\;\frac{A^{2}\,e\sqrt{2\pi n}}{1-2a}\;(2a^{\prime})^{n}\;=\;\frac{A^{2}\,e\sqrt{2\pi n}}{1-2a}\;\alpha^{n},\qquad\alpha:=2a^{\prime}=\frac{2a}{1-2a}. (31)

Since a<14a<\tfrac{1}{4}, we have α<1\alpha<1.

For any η∈(α,1)\eta\in(\alpha,1) the n\sqrt{n} factor in (31) is absorbed into the geometric ratio: n​αn≤Cη​ηn\sqrt{n}\,\alpha^{n}\leq C_{\eta}\,\eta^{n}, where Cη:=supn≥1n​(α/η)n<∞C_{\eta}:=\sup_{n\geq 1}\sqrt{n}\,(\alpha/\eta)^{n}<\infty since α/η<1\alpha/\eta<1. Substituting this into (31) and summing the resulting geometric series over n>Pn>P:

∑n=P+1∞cn2≤A2​e​2​π​Cη1−2​a​ηP+11−η.\sum_{n=P+1}^{\infty}c_{n}^{2}\;\leq\;\frac{A^{2}\,e\sqrt{2\pi}\,C_{\eta}}{1-2a}\;\frac{\eta^{P+1}}{1-\eta}.

Summing over all coordinates (i,k)(i,k) and applying Parseval on the graph eigenbasis (∑j‖Y^n,j‖2=‖Yn‖ℓ2​(V)2=∑i,kcn,i​k2\sum_{j}\|\hat{Y}_{n,j}\|^{2}=\|Y_{n}\|_{\ell^{2}(V)}^{2}=\sum_{i,k}c_{n,ik}^{2}) [29]:

∑n=P+1∞∑j=1N‖Y^n,j‖2≤C​ηP\sum_{n=P+1}^{\infty}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\|\hat{Y}_{n,j}\|^{2}\;\leq\;C\,\eta^{P}

for a constant CC depending on aa, η\eta, and ∑i,kAi​k2\sum_{i,k}A_{ik}^{2}. Now fix any β∈(α,1)\beta\in(\sqrt{\alpha},1) and set η=β2\eta=\beta^{2}. Taking square roots gives

(∑n>P∑j=1N‖Y^n,j‖2)1/2≤Ctr​βP,Ctr:=C.\Big(\sum_{n>P}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\|\hat{Y}_{n,j}\|^{2}\Big)^{1/2}\leq C_{\rm tr}\beta^{P},\qquad C_{\rm tr}:=\sqrt{C}.

Corollary 1 (Readout gap).

‖p¯i−softmax⁡(Zi,0)‖∞≤B2​tr⁡(Σzi),\|\bar{p}_{i}-\mathrm{softmax}(Z_{i,0})\|_{\infty}\;\leq\;\tfrac{B}{2}\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma_{z_{i}}),

and arg⁡maxc⁡p¯i,c=arg⁡maxc​softmax​(Zi,0)c\arg\max_{c}\bar{p}_{i,c}=\arg\max_{c}\mathrm{softmax}(Z_{i,0})_{c} whenever the gap between the two largest entries of softmax⁡(Zi,0)\mathrm{softmax}(Z_{i,0}) exceeds B​tr⁡(Σzi)B\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma_{z_{i}}).

Proof.

Write zi(s)=Zi,0+δi(s)z_{i}^{(s)}=Z_{i,0}+\delta_{i}^{(s)}. Taylor’s theorem with integral remainder gives, for each class cc,

fc(zi(s))=fc(Zi,0)+∇fc(Zi,0)⊤δi(s)+∫01(1−t)(δi(s))⊤∇2fc(Zi,0+tδi(s))δi(s)dt,f_{c}(z_{i}^{(s)})=f_{c}(Z_{i,0})+\nabla f_{c}(Z_{i,0})^{\top}\delta_{i}^{(s)}+\int_{0}^{1}(1-t)\,(\delta_{i}^{(s)})^{\top}\nabla^{2}f_{c}\big(Z_{i,0}+t\delta_{i}^{(s)}\big)\,\delta_{i}^{(s)}\,dt,

Averaging with the quadrature weights, the linear term vanishes because ∑sμs​δi(s)=0\sum_{s}\mu_{s}\delta_{i}^{(s)}=0 (Lemma 3), and ∑sμs​‖δi(s)‖2=tr⁡(Σzi)\sum_{s}\mu_{s}\|\delta_{i}^{(s)}\|^{2}=\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma_{z_{i}}) by the same lemma, which gives the bound. Since (11) penalizes ℰi=tr⁡(Σzi)\mathcal{E}_{i}=\operatorname{tr}(\Sigma_{z_{i}}) on training nodes, the bound is the structural reason the two readouts agree closely in practice (Section 4.2, Table 27). ∎

Appendix B Baseline Details

B.1 Baseline methods

Table 6 summarizes which tasks each method evaluates. G-Δ\DeltaUQ is the closest baseline in scope because it reports all three task families; we compare against it on calibration (Table 1) and distribution shift (Table 4). On OOD detection, the anchor-sampling mechanism in G-Δ\DeltaUQ causes out-of-memory errors in the GNNSafe OOD pipeline, preventing a direct comparison. Across the evaluated benchmarks, the DSS representation gives the strongest calibration and GOOD results among the compared methods, with the best AUROC on 7 of 11 OOD settings. The calibration and GOOD results use plain cross-entropy or ERM training without task-specific robust objectives; in the OOD detection experiments DSS-Hybrid is trained with the same energy-margin objective as GNNSafe++ (Appendix D).

We compare against the following baselines across the three evaluation tasks.

Calibration baselines.

  • •

    TFE-GNN [8]: A spectral GNN that combines three complementary polynomial filters (low-pass, high-pass, and band-pass) via learned attention weights. It uses a propagate-first architecture where spectral filtering is applied once before an MLP backbone.

  • •

    G-Δ\DeltaUQ [33]: An intrinsic uncertainty method that estimates predictive uncertainty through anchor distances in the learned embedding space, without requiring ensembles or Monte Carlo sampling.

OOD detection baselines.

  • •

    GNNSafe [36]: Uses the energy score E(x)=−Tlog∑cexp(zc/T)E(x)=-T\log\sum_{c}\exp(z_{c}/T) as an OOD detection signal, propagated over the graph adjacency to exploit neighborhood consistency. Does not require OOD exposure during training.

  • •

    GNNSafe++ [36]: Extends GNNSafe with an energy-based regularization loss that uses OOD training data to separate in-distribution and OOD energy scores. Uses per-dataset margin hyperparameters (min,mout,λ)(m_{\mathrm{in}},m_{\mathrm{out}},\lambda).

  • •

    Graph-EBM [9]: Models the joint distribution of node features and labels using an energy-based model with graph-aware components, including local and group energy terms propagated through graph diffusion.

  • •

    MC-dropout [10] and Deep Ensembles [17]: Stochastic baselines on the same GCN backbone and training protocol, with M=20M{=}20 dropout passes at test time and M=5M{=}5 independently trained models respectively; both are scored with the same energy score and graph propagation as the energy-based methods (Appendix D).

  • •

    GPN [30]: Graph Posterior Network, an evidential model that propagates per-node Dirichlet evidence over the graph; we report the values obtained on this benchmark by Wu et al. [36].

Distribution-shift baselines.

Table 4 evaluates the GOOD/TAR baselines under concept shift and adds G-Δ\DeltaUQ. Results for ERM through TAR are taken from the TAR paper [38]. Representative baselines include:

  • •

    ERM: Standard empirical risk minimization without any robustness modification.

  • •

    IRM [1]: Invariant Risk Minimization, which penalizes features that are not invariant across training environments.

  • •

    GroupDRO [27]: Distributionally robust optimization that upweights the worst-performing group during training.

  • •

    VREx [16]: Variance Risk Extrapolation, which penalizes variance of risks across training environments.

  • •

    TAR [38]: Topology-Aware Dynamic Reweighting, which uses graph-local transport to reweight training nodes based on loss and neighborhood structure.
