Appendix D Implementation Details

D.1 General training protocol

All DSS-GNN models are trained with the mean-logit cross-entropy loss ℒbase\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{base}} (11); the quadrature-averaged loss

ℒquad=1|𝒱tr|​∑i∈𝒱trℓ¯i+λreg​1|𝒱tr|​∑i∈𝒱trℰi,ℓ¯i=∑s=1Sμs​ℓ​(zi(s),yi),\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{quad}}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{tr}}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{tr}}}\bar{\ell}_{i}\;+\;\lambda_{\mathrm{reg}}\frac{1}{|\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{tr}}|}\sum_{i\in\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{tr}}}\mathcal{E}_{i},\qquad\bar{\ell}_{i}=\sum_{s=1}^{S}\mu_{s}\,\ell(z_{i}^{(s)},y_{i}), (35)

supervises every quadrature node, agrees with ℒbase\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{base}} to first order by Proposition 2, and is used only in that analysis. The loss includes the chaos energy regularizer; λreg\lambda_{\mathrm{reg}} is selected per dataset on validation Brier from {0,10−3,10−2,10−1}\{0,10^{-3},10^{-2},10^{-1}\} (Table 12; Table 17 reports its effect at P=2P{=}2), with 0.010.01 as the default. Training uses early stopping on validation loss with the patience listed per task below. All calibration results report mean ±\pm standard deviation over 10 splits, identical for every method. For the nine datasets above the mid-rule of Table 8 the splits are random with fixed seeds: a class-balanced training set whose per-class quota totals 60% of the nodes when every class is large enough, 20% of the nodes for validation, and the remainder for testing. The five heterophilous-suite datasets use the first 10 public 50/25/25 splits of Platonov et al. [26].

D.2 Calibration (Table 1)

Shared defaults.

Chebyshev filter degrees Klp=Khp=4K_{\mathrm{lp}}{=}K_{\mathrm{hp}}{=}4, chaos order centered at P=2P{=}2 in the base grid, quadrature nodes S=4S{=}4, λreg=0.01\lambda_{\mathrm{reg}}{=}0.01, deterministic scalar gates (Pg=0P_{g}{=}0), loss type = mean, activation = ReLU, learning rate 0.010.01, weight decay 5×10−45{\times}10^{-4}, propagation dropout 0.50.5, linear dropout 0.00.0, epochs 10001000, patience 200200. The best architecture variant per dataset was selected from a grid over propagation type (Chebyshev / TFE-adjacency / propagate-first), graph filter symmetry (symmetric / random-walk), optimizer (Adam / RMSprop), hidden dimension (6464 / 128128), number of layers (22 / 33), and dropout (0.50.5 / 0.60.6 / 0.80.8), evaluated on validation Brier score. Roman-Empire uses hidden 32 and Klp=Khp=2K_{\mathrm{lp}}{=}K_{\mathrm{hp}}{=}2, outside this grid, Minesweeper uses learning rate 0.0050.005, and Chameleon uses sum aggregation. The chaos order PP is a regular hyperparameter selected per dataset on validation Brier over the sweep of Appendix E; Table 12 lists the selected order per dataset together with that single configuration’s accuracy and Brier.

Per-dataset configurations.

Table 11 lists the architecture variant and any hyperparameter overrides from the shared defaults for each dataset.

Selected chaos order per dataset.

Table 12 lists, for each dataset, the chaos order and regularization strength selected on validation Brier, with the accuracy and Brier of that configuration over the same 10 splits, taken from the sweeps of Tables 13 and 14, and its validation Brier (recorded in a separate run of the same configuration on the same splits); Table 1 reports these configurations. DSS-GNN has the best mean Brier on all 14 datasets, including the closest comparisons (Texas 0.2400.240 vs 0.2550.255, Squirrel 0.3940.394 vs 0.3950.395, Amazon-Ratings 0.6340.634 vs 0.6370.637, all TFE-GNN; Questions 0.0530.053 vs 0.0540.054, G-Δ\DeltaUQ). At least one of P=1P{=}1 or P=2P{=}2 is within 0.020.02 Brier of the best swept order on every dataset (Section 4.2), so the larger selected orders are near-ties rather than requirements. The quadrature size is S=4S{=}4 throughout: exact for the polynomial filter and gate terms at P≤3P\leq 3 (Appendix A.1), while at P≥4P\geq 4 the highest-order Hermite products are integrated approximately. The recommended default P=1P{=}1–22 is exact for these terms at S=4S{=}4, and the SS sweep at P=2P{=}2 (Table 18) moves Brier by at most 0.0110.011 on 12 of 14 datasets.

D.3 OOD detection (Section 4.3)

DSS-Hybrid uses a 2-layer GCN base encoder (hidden 64, dropout 0.0) with a DSS residual branch (Klp=3K_{\mathrm{lp}}{=}3, Khp=2K_{\mathrm{hp}}{=}2, P=1P{=}1, S=4S{=}4, deterministic scalar gates). The base encoder is warmed up for 50 epochs before the DSS branch is activated; the residual scale γres\gamma_{\mathrm{res}} is initialized to 0.10.1. All methods run in our pipeline use Adam with learning rate 0.010.01, weight decay 0.010.01, 200 epochs, and 3 seeds, following the GNNSafe protocol. The GNNSafe pipeline uses BatchNorm in its GCN backbones, and so does the DSS-Hybrid base; the standalone model of Appendix G adds per-chaos-channel BatchNorm in all OOD and GOOD cells but OOD Twitch and GOOD-Arxiv/degree. OOD detection scores are computed with the energy score (9) at temperature T=1T{=}1, propagated over the graph adjacency with K=2K{=}2 hops and mixing α=0.5\alpha{=}0.5, following the GNNSafe protocol [36]. DSS-Hybrid is trained with the GNNSafe++ energy-margin regularizer, using the per-dataset margin hyperparameters (min,mout,λ)(m_{\mathrm{in}},m_{\mathrm{out}},\lambda) of Wu et al. [36], as GNNSafe++ is; Graph-EBM, MC-dropout, and Deep Ensembles are trained without it, as GNNSafe is. MC-dropout keeps dropout active at test time with BatchNorm frozen and aggregates M=20M{=}20 stochastic passes; Deep Ensembles aggregate M=5M{=}5 independently initialized backbones; both are scored with the same energy score and propagation as the energy-based methods, applied to the mean logits across passes or members.

Standalone model in the OOD and GOOD pipelines.

For the cross-evaluation of Appendix G, the standalone model adds one BatchNorm1d per chaos channel between hidden DSS layers where noted; Table 1 uses no BatchNorm. The per-cell configurations are listed in Appendix G.

Graph-EBM reproduction.

Graph-EBM is run with a port of the official GraphEBMWrapper [9] at the official default hyperparameters: the multi-scale corrected-conditional energy model with Mahalanobis logit correction, three energy scales, and label-propagation diffusion (diagonal untied covariance, γ=1\gamma{=}1, unit energy weights, α=0.5\alpha{=}0.5 with k=10k{=}10 steps). The scorer is fitted on the same GCN encoder (with BatchNorm, as in the GNNSafe pipeline), trained with the same hyperparameters and seeds as the other baselines run in our pipeline; Graph-EBM’s own diffusion replaces the GNNSafe score propagation for this row. On an exported Cora/structure run (trained GCN logits and embeddings, both graphs, labels, and masks) the port and the official implementation agree at Spearman rank correlation 0.9940.994, and exactly (rank correlation 1.01.0) once the interval and covariance estimators of the official implementation are used.

D.4 Distribution shift (Table 4)

DSS-Hybrid uses a 2-layer GCN base encoder with a DSS residual branch (Klp=3K_{\mathrm{lp}}{=}3, Khp=2K_{\mathrm{hp}}{=}2, P=1P{=}1, S=4S{=}4, hidden 64, deterministic scalar gates, 3 layers total). Training uses Adam with learning rate 10−310^{-3}, weight decay 5×10−45{\times}10^{-4}, dropout 0.50.5, 500 epochs, patience 200. The base encoder is warmed up for 25 epochs. Standard ERM training is used (no robust objective). Published baseline results (ERM through TAR) are taken from the TAR paper [38]; G-Δ\DeltaUQ is run in our pipeline.

D.5 Software, hardware, and compute budget

Experiments use PyTorch and PyTorch Geometric (the released environment pins PyTorch 2.5) on NVIDIA A100 (40 GB) and H100 GPUs; the ogbn-arxiv timing runs of Table 20 use one H100, and the Cornell experiments run on CPU. Mixed precision (FP16) is used for calibration experiments to reduce memory on larger graphs. On the A100 runs, per-epoch wall-clock times range from ∼35{\sim}35 ms (Cora, P=0P{=}0) to ∼650{\sim}650 ms (Amazon-Ratings, P=3P{=}3); see Table 20 for a detailed breakdown.

Compute estimate.

The reported experiments (calibration: 14 datasets ×\times 10 runs; OOD: 5 datasets ×\times 3 seeds; GOOD: 7 settings) total approximately 8 A100 GPU-hours. The ablation studies (chaos order PP, regularization λreg\lambda_{\mathrm{reg}}, quadrature nodes SS, and contribution decomposition; Appendix E) add approximately 100 GPU-hours. Hyperparameter selection (grid search over architecture variant, hidden dimension, optimizer, and dropout) required an additional ∼25{\sim}25 GPU-hours. The total compute for the project, including preliminary experiments not reported in the paper, is approximately 200 A100 GPU-hours.

Code is available at https://github.com/heraclixus/DSSGNN.

Appendix E Ablation Study Details

E.1 Polynomial order PP across all datasets

Figure 3 summarizes the chaos-order sweep referenced in Section 4.2, and Tables 13 and 14 report the per-dataset classification accuracy and Brier score for DSS-GNN across all 14 datasets for P∈{0,1,2,3,4,5,6,8}P\in\{0,1,2,3,4,5,6,8\}. All results are mean ±\pm standard deviation over 10 random splits. For each dataset, the best-performing PP is highlighted in bold.

On four datasets the best swept order exceeds two (PubMed, Squirrel, Amazon-Ratings, and Minesweeper); on every dataset P=1P=1 or P=2P=2 is within 0.02 Brier of the best swept value.

E.2 Chaos order on OOD detection and under distribution shift

OOD detection.

Varying only the chaos order P∈{0,1,2,3}P\in\{0,1,2,3\} in the DSS-Hybrid OOD configuration (GCN base, energy score with propagation, energy-margin training, every other hyperparameter fixed; 3 runs) leaves energy AUROC flat: Cora-structure 91.0/91.2/90.9/90.891.0/91.2/90.9/90.8 and Amazon-Photo/feature 99.4/99.5/99.5/99.599.4/99.5/99.5/99.5 for P=0,1,2,3P=0,1,2,3, Coauthor-CS likewise flat, and on ogbn-arxiv the AUROC moves by at most 0.80.8 across P=0P=0 to 33 (the runs of Table 20). The absolute levels differ from Table 2 because the ablation is a separate set of runs at one configuration per dataset. This is the behavior the design predicts: the energy score reads the mean logit alone (9), so PP can be selected for calibration without affecting detection, and the detection margin comes from the DSS representation under a fixed readout (Section 4.3).

Distribution shift.

At the validation-selected standalone configurations of Appendix G, Table 15 varies only PP (3 seeds). P=1P{=}1 is the argmax on both the OOD-validation and the test split on all three settings, so at these configurations the chaos order contributes +1.7+1.7, +1.2+1.2, and +0.6+0.6 points of shifted accuracy over the deterministic P=0P{=}0 arm.

E.3 Energy-score propagation

Table 16 isolates the score-propagation step of the energy readout on DSS-Hybrid: the raw energy and the propagated energy are computed from the same trained checkpoints (one fixed configuration, 3 runs), so the difference is due to propagation alone. Propagation helps on 9 of 11 settings, by up to +18.2+18.2 AUROC (Twitch) and +14.5+14.5 (Cora-structure); the two exceptions are Cora/label (−6.7-6.7), where the fixed smoothing averages away part of the leave-out signal inside homophilous neighborhoods, and Amazon-Photo/structure (−0.4-0.4), at noise level. The same step transfers to the standalone model (Cora/label +0.9+0.9, Amazon-Photo/label +13.4+13.4 at identical checkpoints). We apply propagation uniformly for protocol parity with GNNSafe++.

E.4 Chaos energy regularization λreg\lambda_{\mathrm{reg}}

Table 17 reports the Brier score as the chaos energy regularization strength λreg\lambda_{\mathrm{reg}} varies from 0 to 0.1 with P=2P=2 fixed. Each column is an independent set of 10-split runs; at each dataset’s selected λreg\lambda_{\mathrm{reg}} the cell agrees with the P=2P{=}2 column of Table 14 within one standard deviation. The regularizer of (11) penalizes large chaos coefficients; at λreg=0\lambda_{\mathrm{reg}}=0 the chaos expansion is still active (all P+1P+1 channels are learned), but without an explicit energy penalty. Moderate regularization (λreg∈{10−3,10−2}\lambda_{\mathrm{reg}}\in\{10^{-3},10^{-2}\}) yields the best calibration on the majority of datasets. On Texas, λreg\lambda_{\mathrm{reg}} matters most (0.3660.366 at 00 versus 0.2130.213 at 10−210^{-2}); on Citeseer, Wisconsin, and Roman-Empire λreg=0\lambda_{\mathrm{reg}}{=}0 is best and larger values degrade Brier, which is why λreg\lambda_{\mathrm{reg}} is selected per dataset on validation Brier.

E.5 Number of quadrature nodes SS

Table 18 reports the Brier score as the number of Gauss–Hermite quadrature nodes SS varies from 2 to 8, with P=2P=2 fixed. Each column is an independent set of 10-split runs; the S=4S{=}4 column agrees with the P=2P{=}2 column of Table 14 within one standard deviation. For the deterministic gates used in these runs (Pg=0P_{g}=0), the theoretical minimum for exact chaos arithmetic at P=2P=2 is S≥⌈(Pg+2​P+1)/2⌉=3S\geq\lceil(P_{g}+2P+1)/2\rceil=3 (Appendix A.1). Brier varies by at most 0.0110.011 across S∈{2,…,8}S\in\{2,\dots,8\} on 12 of 14 datasets. The exceptions are Wisconsin, where S=2S{=}2, below the theoretical minimum, gives a higher Brier score (0.1420.142 vs 0.1090.109 at S=3S{=}3), consistent with the exactness requirement of Theorem 3, and Cornell, where the spread across SS (0.2180.218 to 0.2860.286) is within one standard deviation of its 10-split results. The chaos-order sweeps of Tables 13–14 use S=4S{=}4 throughout, exact for P≤3P\leq 3; at P≥4P\geq 4 the highest-order Hermite products are integrated approximately (Appendix D).

E.6 Contribution decomposition: backbone vs. chaos

Table 19 decomposes the calibration improvement into two factors: the graph-spectral backbone and the chaos expansion. The “ChebNet” column reports a vanilla single-branch Chebyshev filter (K=4K{=}4, hidden 64) as a diagnostic backbone baseline, not as part of the main uncertainty-aware baseline comparison in Table 1. The “P=0P{=}0” column uses the Table 1 architecture for each dataset (which may include propagate-first or dual branches) with the chaos expansion disabled. The “Best P>0P{>}0” column adds the chaos expansion on the same architecture. The P=0→P>0P{=}0\to P{>}0 comparison is strictly fair (same architecture, only PP changes) and shows that the chaos expansion improves calibration on 12 of 14 datasets (3.63.6–27.9%27.9\% Brier reduction), indicating that the stochastic expansion is the primary source of the calibration gains over the P=0P{=}0 version in this controlled comparison. The ChebNet column gives useful context: on the small WebKB datasets Texas and Wisconsin, the single-filter ChebNet attains a lower absolute Brier score, while the controlled P=0P{=}0 versus P>0P{>}0 comparison still isolates the contribution of the chaos expansion. The ChebNet column is also the single-filter control for the filtering design: at P=0P{=}0 the per-dataset dual-filter architecture has lower or equal Brier than the single-branch ChebNet on 12 of 14 datasets (equal on Questions; Chameleon 0.3620.362 vs 0.7760.776, Squirrel 0.4160.416 vs 0.7980.798, Roman-Empire 0.2980.298 vs 0.3680.368), with Texas and Wisconsin as the exceptions noted above.

E.7 Computational overhead

Asymptotic complexity.

Although the doubly-spectral expansion is defined on the tensor product ℓ2​(V)⊗L2​(ℝ,γ)\ell^{2}(V)\otimes L^{2}(\mathbb{R},\gamma), truncating the chaos basis at order PP retains only P+1P{+}1 coefficients along the stochastic axis, so the graph-filtering cost and the coefficient memory scale as (P+1)×(P{+}1)\times the deterministic ChebNet baseline and the node-wise dense cost as S×S\times. Concretely, one DSS layer takes 𝒪⁡((P+1)​(Klp+Khp)​|E|​d+S​N​d2+S⁡(P+1)​N​d)\mathcal{O}\!\big((P{+}1)(K_{\mathrm{lp}}+K_{\mathrm{hp}})|E|d+SNd^{2}+S(P{+}1)Nd\big) time and 𝒪⁡((P+1+S)​N​d)\mathcal{O}((P{+}1+S)Nd) memory, where |E||E| is the number of edges, dd the hidden width, and SS the number of Gauss–Hermite quadrature nodes; the chaos extension is therefore additive, not combinatorial, in the stochastic direction, and no eigendecomposition is ever computed. With SS at the exactness threshold (S=P+1S=P+1) the quadrature term is quadratic in PP; this is the worst-case operation count, and the measured growth in PP is much smaller (below). By Theorem 2 the truncation error decays exponentially in PP for targets satisfying the growth condition of Appendix A.6, consistent with the empirical plateau at P=1P{=}1–22, so the constant factor over a deterministic backbone stays small. All chaos coefficients share the same Chebyshev filters and projection weights, so the parameter count per layer is 𝒪⁡(Klp+Khp+(P+1)​(Pg+1)+dℓ​dℓ+1)\mathcal{O}\big(K_{\mathrm{lp}}+K_{\mathrm{hp}}+(P{+}1)(P_{g}{+}1)+d_{\ell}d_{\ell+1}\big) (filter coefficients, gate coefficients an,r,bn,ra_{n,r},b_{n,r}, and the linear map); the chaos order enters only through the gate coefficients and the input lift. By contrast, the MC-dropout and Deep Ensemble baselines require MM forward passes or models at inference (M=20M{=}20 and M=5M{=}5 in our comparisons).

Wall-clock measurements.

Table 20 reports the wall-clock time per training epoch as the chaos order PP increases, on three datasets spanning two orders of magnitude in size. The overhead grows linearly with PP: each additional chaos order adds one extra graph filter evaluation and Gauss–Hermite projection per layer. At P=2P=2 the per-epoch cost ranges from 2.9×2.9\times on Cora to 1.2×1.2\times on Amazon-Ratings and 1.1×1.1\times on ogbn-arxiv relative to the deterministic baseline (P=0P=0), within the asymptotic bound above and well below the M×M\times overhead of MC-dropout or ensembles. The measured overhead decreases as graphs grow because the per-order arithmetic is batched into single kernels, and on larger graphs fixed per-epoch costs and better accelerator utilization account for a larger share of the epoch time. On ogbn-arxiv (169K nodes, one H100 GPU) each additional chaos order adds about 4%4\% per-epoch time, and peak GPU memory grows linearly in P+1P{+}1 (1.68/2.75/3.88/5.021.68/2.75/3.88/5.02 GiB for P=0,…,3P=0,\dots,3), consistent with the memory analysis above; peak memory on Cora is 75.975.9 MiB.

E.8 Summary of component evidence

Table 21 collects, for each architectural component, the controlled comparison that isolates it and the effect measured. The chaos expansion improves calibration (and, at the selected GOOD configurations, shifted accuracy); the spectral filtering design and the residual improve accuracy under heterophily and shift; the energy score with propagation provides OOD detection. Each task’s readout uses a different part of the same representation.

Appendix F Comparison with Standard GNN Baselines

Table 1 in the main text compares DSS-GNN against recent uncertainty-aware graph methods (TFE-GNN and G-Δ\DeltaUQ). Here we additionally compare against GCN [15] and GAT [34], two widely used GNN architectures that do not incorporate any uncertainty mechanism. Both baselines use 2 layers, 64 hidden units, Adam optimizer (lr==0.01, weight decay==5×\times10-4), and the same 10 splits as DSS-GNN.

Table 23 reports accuracy and Brier score. The main observation is that higher accuracy does not imply better calibration. On Cora, GCN and GAT both achieve higher accuracy than DSS-GNN (87.5%87.5\% and 87.8%87.8\% vs. 86.6%86.6\%) yet have worse Brier scores (0.2130.213 and 0.2220.222 vs. 0.2070.207). On Citeseer, GAT matches DSS-GNN in accuracy (80.6%80.6\% vs. 80.2%80.2\%) but is substantially worse in Brier (0.3530.353 vs. 0.3080.308). On many heterophilous benchmarks, GCN and GAT have much lower accuracy and higher Brier scores than DSS-GNN. The calibration gains of DSS-GNN are therefore not an accuracy effect.

Stochastic baselines under the same protocol.

Table 22 adds MC-dropout (M=20M{=}20 stochastic passes at test time, probabilities averaged) and Deep Ensembles (M=5M{=}5 independently trained models, probabilities averaged) on the GCN of Table 23, under the full 10-split protocol and the same code path; the plain-GCN control from that code path reproduces Table 23 (Cora 87.4787.47 vs 87.4587.45, Wisconsin 50.2550.25 vs 50.2550.25). DSS-GNN’s Brier is lower on all 14 datasets than either baseline, and ensembling improves the GCN’s Brier by at most 0.0080.008 on any dataset while MC-dropout sometimes worsens it (Cora): averaging a conventional GNN does not remove the calibration difference. On Cora and Questions the margins are small (0.2070.207 vs 0.2130.213 and 0.0530.053 vs 0.0550.055). The same multi-pass cost structure applies to sampling-based Bayesian GNNs and latent-variable GNNs; the chaos expansion is instead deterministic, with no sampling variance.

Appendix G Cross-Evaluation of the Two Deployment Modes

This appendix gives the full tables for Section 4.5: the hybrid under the calibration protocol, the standalone model under the OOD and GOOD protocols, the readout-coincidence measurement of Section 4.2, the effect of BatchNorm under the calibration protocol, and the covariate-shift counterpart of Table 4.

Table 5 (Section 4.5) summarizes both deployment modes on all three tasks; the per-dataset comparisons summarized in its cells are Tables 24, 25, and 26 below.

G.1 Protocols

Hybrid under the calibration protocol.

DSS-Hybrid (2-layer GCN base with the DSS residual branch of Appendix D) is trained under the identical 10-split protocol of Table 1, paired with its own GCN base trained identically with the residual removed and matched budgets, so the pair isolates the residual branch.

Standalone under the OOD protocol.

Standalone DSS-GNN is trained in the GNNSafe pipeline (200 epochs, 3 runs, energy score with propagation, pipeline defaults: hidden 64, 2 layers, weight decay 10−210^{-2}, learning rate 10−210^{-2}, P=1P{=}1, S=4S{=}4). Rows marked ++BN add the per-chaos-channel BatchNorm of Appendix D, with every other hyperparameter unchanged; the variant is selected on the validation split. Twitch uses learning rate 10−310^{-3}, hidden 128, and no BatchNorm, selected on validation ID accuracy. The Arxiv row is trained with the GNNSafe++ energy-margin objective at the Arxiv margin hyperparameters of Wu et al. [36] with mout=−1m_{\mathrm{out}}{=}-1, selected on validation ID accuracy. All other rows use standard ID training.

Standalone under the GOOD protocol.

Standalone DSS-GNN is trained in the GOOD pipeline with L1L_{1} row-normalized input features, 2 layers, Klp=3K_{\mathrm{lp}}{=}3, Khp=2K_{\mathrm{hp}}{=}2, 500 epochs, patience 200, 3 seeds; the epoch is selected by OOD-validation loss within each run and the configuration (BatchNorm on/off, learning rate, hidden width, PP) on the GOOD OOD-validation split: CBAS and WebKB ++BN, learning rate 10−210^{-2}; Twitch ++BN, 10−310^{-3}; GOOD-Cora/word ++BN, 5×10−35\times 10^{-3}, hidden 128, weight decay 10−310^{-3}; GOOD-Cora/degree ++BN, 3×10−33\times 10^{-3}, hidden 128; GOOD-Arxiv/time ++BN, 10−210^{-2}, hidden 256; GOOD-Arxiv/degree no BatchNorm, 10−210^{-2}, hidden 64; P=1P{=}1 throughout.

G.2 Calibration: standalone, hybrid, and the hybrid’s GCN base

The hybrid is at or above its own base on 11 of 14 datasets in accuracy; the three negative deltas (Texas −0.82-0.82, Chameleon −0.50-0.50, Wisconsin −0.38-0.38) are far inside one standard deviation, and every positive Brier delta (hybrid worse) is at most 0.00080.0008, also far inside one standard deviation. The gains are structural and large where the GCN inductive bias fails: Roman-Empire +27.7+27.7 accuracy and −0.33-0.33 Brier, Minesweeper +6.6+6.6 and −0.11-0.11, Tolokers +1.7+1.7 and −0.04-0.04. On the small heterophilous graphs where the GCN backbone itself fails (Texas, Cornell, Wisconsin, Chameleon, Squirrel), the residual matches the base rather than improving on it, and the standalone model is the deployment choice. In hybrid mode the argmax of the quadrature predictive and of the mean logit agree on every test node of every dataset (disagreement 0.00000.0000 on all 14).

G.3 OOD detection: standalone versus hybrid

∗Table 2 reports AUROC only. Hybrid ID accuracy on these nine settings (3 runs under the same protocol) is Cora 81.6/81.1/90.681.6/81.1/90.6, Amazon-Photo 92.4/91.0/95.492.4/91.0/95.4, Coauthor-CS 93.0/93.0/95.593.0/93.0/95.5 (structure/feature/label).

The hybrid is the stronger detector on 10 of 11 settings; the standalone trains on all 11 (ID accuracies in Table 25) and is competitive on the label-shift settings (Cora/label 94.0394.03 vs 94.1194.11) and on Arxiv, where under the GNNSafe++ margin objective it reaches 73.7373.73 AUROC, above the hybrid’s 73.3673.36, with the best Arxiv ID accuracy of any method in Table 3 (61.1661.16). The one standalone exception is Twitch: the classifier itself trains (ID accuracy 68.3968.39 vs the hybrid’s 70.5270.52), but its energy score does not separate the cross-graph OOD inputs, so the hybrid (95.7595.75) is preferred there. The per-chaos-channel BatchNorm of Appendix D is used on all nine perturbation settings, where the sparse public splits require it for every backbone in the pipeline (Section 4.5).

G.4 Distribution shift: standalone versus hybrid

The standalone model is above every baseline of Table 4 on 5 of 7 settings (WebKB, Twitch, Cora word, Cora degree, Arxiv degree) and at ERM’s level on the remaining two (ERM: 82.4382.43 on CBAS and 65.6465.64 on Arxiv/time), while the hybrid is above every baseline on all 7; on GOOD-Cora/word the two modes agree within noise (64.8164.81 vs 64.89±0.2164.89\pm 0.21). GOOD-CBAS is a small synthetic graph with the largest seed variance of the seven settings (standalone SD 13.213.2 over 3 seeds). ID accuracies of the standalone runs are between 63.563.5 and 96.296.2 across the seven settings (CBAS 96.296.2, WebKB 76.076.0, Twitch 63.563.5, Cora word 68.868.8, Cora degree 68.968.9, Arxiv time 74.174.1, Arxiv degree 71.571.5).

G.5 Readout coincidence

Table 27 compares the two readouts of Section 3.2 at identical checkpoints.

G.6 BatchNorm under the calibration protocol

Table 28 re-runs the Table 1 protocol with and without the per-chaos-channel BatchNorm on four datasets (10 splits each). The BatchNorm-free controls reproduce Table 1 within a fraction of one standard deviation (the Citeseer run uses the selected P=2P{=}2 configuration of Table 12, with λreg=0\lambda_{\mathrm{reg}}{=}0, and reproduces that row as well). With BatchNorm, Cora and Roman-Empire are unchanged within noise and Wisconsin is within one standard deviation, while Citeseer degrades far beyond noise (−13.2-13.2 accuracy). BatchNorm is therefore a stabilization for the sparse-label OOD pipeline, where every baseline backbone also uses it, and is not used under the full-label calibration protocol.

G.7 Covariate shift on GOOD

Table 29 is the covariate-shift counterpart of Table 4: the same seven GOOD settings under their covariate splits, comparing ERM-trained DSS-Hybrid (GCN encoder, configuration selected by validation loss) with the same-protocol ERM GCN of the GNNSafe pipeline (3 seeds). DSS-Hybrid is above the ERM control on 6 of 7 settings; the one loss, GOOD-Cora/degree, is within 1.81.8 points. The two Arxiv ERM baselines did not converge within the shared 120-epoch budget (ID accuracy 45 to 50, versus 72 to 77 for the DSS runs on the same splits), so those two margins are not informative on their own. With the seven concept-shift settings of Table 4 this covers both shift families that GOOD defines.
